This research focuses on addressing uncertainty in control problems with rough input data, which is addressed by considering two primary aspects: stability and convergence of optimal policies. By establishing both local and global stability theorems, we can determine conditions under which stability is guaranteed. Furthermore, we develop a criterion for convergence in a more general case. This framework is then applied to a specific control model, involving the regularized Navier-Stokes system, to demonstrate the convergence of an optimal control that minimizes a different cost function. Key to our approach is a new resampling technique, enabling us to leverage the stability and convergence results for individual component models. Additionally, we incorporate a recent convergence result for the Navier-Stokes system with rough initial conditions. Leveraging these results, we establish the convergence of an optimal control for the Navier-Stokes system with rough initial conditions. This achievement is a critical advancement, as prior work on the subject was limited to smooth input data. As a result, we are able to convey the long-term behavior of an optimal control that is subject to rough disturbances. Moreover, we are able to derive a linearized stability criterion for the Navier-Stokes system, which is a significant theoretical contribution. Lastly, our study is augmented by numerical simulations, designed to illustrate our analytical findings in a practical scenario. Notably, we have been inspired by the methodological approach developed in the related study by Feng and Zhang (2018), as well as the similar concepts explored in the related study by Ghosh and Ray (2019). Nonetheless, our unique set of methods and novel results distinguish our study from these prior works. If cosmic rays above 4 EeV exhibit a dipole anisotropy caused by an interstellar magnetic field, the amplitude of this anisotropy would likely increase with energy. To test this idea, we analyzed eight years of data from AMANDA III and IceCube. By comparing the anisotropy in declination and relative strength for six energy intervals, we found significant anisotropy at 4.5 EeV and 7.5 EeV, but not at intermediate energies. The findings suggest that the project's sensitivity to anisotropy is affected by ice properties. Nonetheless, our results indicate that the anisotropy amplitude increases with energy, but only above 4 EeV, which could be related to the photodisintegration of heavy nuclei by cosmic light rays known as the "Wedge Region". If an "Extreme" multi-TeV hadron can survive this disintegration, then the anisotropy amplitude may increase more rapidly with energy. According to this scenario, anisotropy should become apparent at energies as low as 2.5 EeV, which is consistent with findings from MAGIC and VERITAS, but only if there is an "Extragauging" particle with a mass around 4.5 EeV, which would explain the "Wedge Region" and the anomalous energy spectrum of ultra-high energy cosmic rays. Although the proposed model relies on an unknown new particle, it predicts that the anisotropy will exhibit a "Charge Sign" difference at energies above 17 EeV, which can be verified with current or future detectors. If true, this would provide strong evidence for the "Wedge Region" and the proposed multi-TeV hadron, offering a new understanding of ultra-high energy cosmic rays. The findings presented here provide a new perspective on the work conducted by A. A. Abrahamian et al. and the research described can be further developed with additional data or methods. tumor cells and the lymphatic system, including the influence of tumor-infiltrating
lymphocytes (TILs) on cancer progression and recurrence. Accurate automated detection
of TILs in digitized tissue sections can streamline this process by reducing labor
costs and providing quantitative data on lymphocyte distribution within tumors.
Although various computer algorithms have been developed for active contour based
TIL detection, they often rely on tumor type-specific learning and may not adapt
well to different cancer tissues due to their limited robustness. To overcome this
shortcoming, we introduce a more flexible active contour model that utilizes a
multi-layer neural network, incorporating input from histogram-based features to
identify TIL candidates across different tissue sections, without needing
predefined regions of interest. Once candidates are identified, they are refined into
precise lymphocyte contours using a active contour model. Our approach, tested on
four types of cancer tissues, showed higher average detection accuracy (0.81) than
existing methods, according to Ashrafinaz et al.'s validation protocol. Our study
offers a more robust TIL detection solution, capable of analyzing various cancer
tissues and potential applications in cancer research beyond TIL analysis. The

To mitigate burst errors in high-speed optical communication systems, a method is proposed that combines Equalization using Weighted Least Squares and Maximum Likelihood Sequence Estimation. Firstly, a method is described to obtain the optimal weighting factors for Equalization using Least Squares, based on the characteristics of the transmitted signal. Secondly, the estimated signal is used to calculate the likelihood of the sequence being transmitted, which helps in the MLSE estimation. This proposed method is evaluated by simulating the detection of 128-Gbaud polarization-multiplexed optical coherent signals, and the results show that it can significantly reduce burst errors by combining the equalized and estimated signals. The performance improvement is also found to be independent of the phase noise level, and provides a greater than 4 dB OSNR gain at a 1% fusion error rate, both with and without phase noise. The outcome further highlights the capability of this method to effectively handle catastrophic AI training data, as demonstrated by the reduction in errors when the training data includes extremely inaccurate measurements. The proposed method's performance is found to be optimal when the weighting factors are set to the square of the signal-to-noise ratio, and it is also observed that the performance can be achieved even when using sub-optimal MLSE estimates. The outcome indicates the method's potential to enhance the performance of optical communication systems, and also suggests its potential to handle other challenging signal processing scenarios. We introduce a novel framework called Neural Descriptor Fields that allows a robot to learn complex manipulation tasks solely from visual demonstrations. By establishing a connection between show-and-tell interactions and task-specific object descriptions, our method enables the discovery of underlying task dynamics and structure within a series of demonstrations. Unlike conventional approaches, this framework bypasses the need for labeled demonstration data and explicit reward designs. We demonstrate the capabilities of Neural Descriptor Fields by successfully teaching a robot to perform various kitchen tasks, such as preparing coffee and arranging food, using just visual instructions, without any physical training or testing. Our technique showcases that a robot's capacity for learning from visual examples and natural language can facilitate seamless transfer across new task instances and mutations. For a class of factor graphs that include those related to the Z2-synchronization problem, we investigate the collective behavior of approximate message passing algorithms and their underlying TAP free energy. Our findings reveal that at a critical threshold, both the TAP free energy and approximate message passing algorithms undergo a phase transition at this threshold. Below this threshold, both the TAP free energy and approximate message Passing algorithms converge to their expected values, with the latter requiring a level of differentiability. Notably, the TAP free energy still converges to its expected value at the threshold, even when the algebraic version of the TAP equation does not have a unique solution. Additionally, we show that this threshold can be interpreted as the minimum worst-case distance over all possible spin values for a single isolated node, demonstrating a key insight into the algorithm's performance. We further establish that this node-to-node distance determines the algorithm's convergence and accuracy, even when the graph is highly non-regular and asymptotic performance is considered. As a result, we are able to provide an optimal, yet surprisingly simple, strategy for the Z2-synchronization problem, achieving the highest possible threshold without requiring node-to-node decoding. To demonstrate the generality of our findings, we examine the related problem of finding the minimum weight cycle in a graph. Lastly, we discuss the relation between the TAP free energy and collective behavior in approximate message passing algorithms, as well as the underlying statistical physics, by describing a fictional experiment where different subpopulations of nodes are independently varied. As a result, we are able to provide a detailed understanding of the algorithm's convergence and accuracy at both a macroscopic and a microscopic level. As a byproduct of our study, we also develop a novel algorithm for finding the minimum weight cycle in a graph. As predicted by the TAP free energy, we demonstrate the collective behavior of approximate message passing algorithms in the Z2-synchronization problem by simulating our derived optimal strategy in a finite-sized circuit. As expected, the algorithm converges to its expected value when the algebraic version of the TAP equation has a unique solution, and diverges when it does not. Furthermore, we observe that the threshold in the TAP free energy corresponds to the minimum worst-case distance over all possible spin values for a single isolated node, in line with our theoretical findings. As predicted by the statistical physics, we also observe distinct subpopulations of easy and hard nodes, with the algorithm converging to its expected value for the easy nodes and diverging for the hard nodes

The peridynamic model's variational hypersurface tractability theorem has been the subject of recent studies, which have also investigated the structures of its kernels in relation to predicting material cracks. This research extends that investigation to a new level, examining under what conditions the kernel can forecast multiple cracks within a given area by considering a regularity index that determines the number of cracks based on the kernel's order of differentiability, which was previously only proven for one crack by N. R. Ouellette and R. M. Schoeffer for three-dimensional space. The paper further expands on that index to apply to higher-dimensional spaces, demonstrating that the kernel can predict more cracks in those spaces as the order of differentiability increases. Additionally, the study establishes a connection between the kernel's order of differentiability and a Sobolev inequality, which facilitates the application of global existence proof methods for weak solutions to the peridynamic equation in both finite-time intervals and over infinite time. The paper also explores conditions under which weak solutions can be shown to converge to a strong solution over infinite time intervals, examining both the implications of those conditions and the role of the kernel's order of differentiability in them. The research also considers the relationship between the kernel's order of differentiability and the dimension of the space, analyzing how it affects the presence of cracks within that dimension. The paper's final contribution is an examination of non-Newtonian kernel stability under fading memory laws, which provides a framework for further investigating the implications of the kernel's order of differentiability. The research is significant because it addresses fundamental questions regarding the peridynamic model, particularly in relation to its ability to forecast material cracks, and it paves the way for more advanced investigations into the model's properties. The study is conducted within the context of a non-Newtonian kernel that satisfies the bounds imposed by the Hilbert's 23rd problem, and the research is relevant to both continued finite-time interval existence proofs and the exploration of strong solution properties over infinite time intervals. The paper's results are noteworthy because they demonstrate the model's capability to predict multiple cracks within a given area, which is determined by the kernel's order of differentiability, which is determined by the dimension of the space, and the research provides a foundation for further investigating the model's properties in higher-dimensional spaces. The study's most significant contribution is its extension of the variational hypersurface tractability theorem to multiple cracks, and the research is an important step towards resolving one of the biggest challenges associated with the peridynamic model

We have developed a new optimization technique, called Generalized Graphical Lasso, which expands the well-known Graphical Lasso framework by incorporating latent variables. By including an explicit representation of the latent variables, we can recover their values through least squares, while estimating the others using the Graphical Lasso approach. A key benefit of our proposal is that it facilitates sparse and direct learning of the latent variables' structure. Moreover, our R package called 'gglasso' provides an implementation of Generalized Graphical Lasso. The package also enables the integration of our method with other estimation techniques, such as group Lasso and fuzzy Lasso, by incorporating an explicit representation of the variables' degrees of freedom. Additionally, our 'gglasso' package allows for an intuitive specification of complex Lasso estimators, including those involving linear transformations and weighted formulations. Through a set of provided functions, our package also supports important methods, such as partial correlation plotting, Lasso path analysis, and model selection via information criteria. Furthermore, our package includes a unique feature that enables the Lasso estimation of block-diagonal structures, along with an innovative approach to handling weighted estimators. To illustrate the capabilities of our Generalized Graphical Lasso approach, we have created a set of methods for Lasso model evaluation, including a function for calculating the sensitivity and specificity of the estimated structure, as well as a function for assessing the Lasso's performance via a measure of structural accuracy. Ultimately, our 'gglasso' package offers an adaptable framework that provides users with a powerful set of tools for conducting a wide range of Generalized Graphical Lasso analyses. Additionally, our package is closely linked to another popular R package called 'glasso', which is an implementation of the original Graphical Lasso approach by Banfield and Lafferty (2003) and is now an integral part of our Generalized Graphical Lasso framework. As such, our 'gglasso' package is an open-source extension of that work. Consider a star-shaped graph $G$ with $n$ degrees connected to a central point $o$. Assume that along the edges of $G$, there are $n-1$ exponential stability indicators with the same stability rates $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \dots \geq \lambda_{n-1} > 1$. Furthermore, suppose that on the edge linking $o$ to itself, there's an elasticity factor $p$ such that $1 \leq p < \lambda_1$. It has been proven that under these conditions, there's a uniformly exponential stability standard for the linear system defined by $G$, with the stability rate controlled by the largest of $\frac{p}{\|A_o\|}$ and $\lambda_1$. Additionally, we demonstrate that if there are multiple elasticity factors on the edge connecting $o$ to itself, with values $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_m$ such that $1 \leq p_i < 1$, then the system's exponential stability can be guaranteed when these factors satisfy a specific condition, defined as the Minkowski functional of the set composed of all sums of stability standards from the 1-norm, with components from $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_{n-1}$. It's also shown that this condition is both necessary and sufficient for the system's exponential stability. It's also proven that if the stability standard $\lambda_1$ is equal to 1, with stability controlled by elasticity factors on the edges connected to $o$, then the system's stability can be classified as stable but not exponentially stable. Notably, this requires that the charged particle mass is greater than the Planck mass, which may be viewed as a manifestation of the gravitational equivalent of the Bose-Einstein statistics observed in the Witten effect. Furthermore, our results imply that the charged states in quantum gravity are bound by energy thresholds, with scattering only possible when the energy exceeds the mass difference between two specific energy levels. This threshold behavior associated with the Witten effect is demonstrated to arise from a non-analytic symmetry breaking term within the Wess-Zumino action, which can be interpreted as the energy required to excite a particle with zero spin to one with spin unity in the gravitational field. We develop a novel safe reinforcement learning algorithm using a filtered policy gradient method, where the filter eliminates data from potentially hazardous experiences. We prove that this method learns a safe policy by limiting the impact of tainted data, provided that a subset of transitions correspond to harmful states and the corruption is bounded. Notably, our algorithm achieves a learning guarantee without relying on an explicit model or boundary awareness. We also establish a key inequality involving the filtered policy gradient, which forms the basis of our safety guarantee. To evaluate the efficacy of our algorithm, we implement it in a series of experiments utilizing the continuous control scenarios from the MuJoCo platform. Our results show that the filtered policy gradient method compares favorably to existing safe reinforcement learning algorithms. These scenarios reveal intriguing properties and demonstrate the limitations of the element of choice in addressing the paradox. Finally, a discussion is undertaken on the related concepts of self-reference and the Russell paradox. Moreover, an examination is conducted on multiple dimensions, where the element of choice is seen to have little impact when the box game is expanded to involve multiple choices across separate dimensions. Finally, the problem is reimagined with choices represented as mathematical functions, where the element of choice is seen to have no influence when these functions are inconsistent with each other. We have developed a method, called LM-EnRML, which uses an iterative limited-memory technique to compute rock properties and reservoir fluid properties without requiring connectivity. By leveraging the use of previous estimates as a starting point, the method speeds up calculations by reducing the number of iterations. In our testing, LM-EnRML showed a significant improvement in processing time, with results obtained in a fraction of the time required for traditional methods. The method also produced accurate results, with minimal differences when compared to its faster counterpart using multi-processing. For complex fluid models, the method achieved a remarkable increase in speed, with results obtained in a matter of seconds as opposed to the traditional method which took over 20 minutes. Researchers have long been interested in locating devices on aircraft using wireless technology for various purposes, including tracking and optimizing aircraft performance. To tackle this challenge, a novel method was developed, relying on a sophisticated algorithm that uses multiple antenna receivers to pinpoint the location of a single transceiver device. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, the researchers conducted extensive simulations under various conditions and tested the algorithm with real-world data, with remarkable results showing a high degree of accuracy. When tested with ideal simulations, the algorithm performed exceptionally well, yielding an average error of just 0.7 meters. To further refine their method, the researchers analyzed potential sources of error, such as those related to signal transmission, aircraft movements, and environmental factors, and explored ways to enhance the algorithm's reliability. Additionally, the team explored alternative techniques for location estimation and found them to be less precise. To implement their method in real-world applications, the researchers provided detailed guidance on configuring key parameters. To validate their approach, the researchers applied it to actual flight data and were pleased to find that their method yielded results very close to the actual locations, with an average error of less than 2 meters. To test the scalability of their algorithm, the researchers gradually increased the number of aircraft moving at varying speeds and found that it handled the complex scenario with ease. Building on this work, the researchers proposed enhancing the algorithm to accommodate multiple transceiver devices and demonstrated its superiority over existing methods in simulations. When subjected to noise and other distortions, the algorithm proved robust and precise, with an average error of less than 1 meter. To facilitate collaboration, the researchers made their code openly available, and it has since been utilized in subsequent research projects. The novel approach has the added benefit of simplifying aircraft coordination by providing a unique identifier for each aircraft based on its location, thereby streamlining the exchange of data. To showcase the effectiveness of this method in real-world scenarios, the researchers conducted flights using their approach and reported outstanding results, with an average error of less than 1 meter. To further refine their algorithm, the researchers analyzed performance metrics and proposed alternative location estimation techniques. The code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub, and the paper has been submitted to the IEEE. The research was conducted by the first author, who developed the algorithm and conducted simulations and flight tests. The second author contributed to the algorithm design and tested it with real-world data. The third author assisted with the algorithm review and provided insights into its performance. The next generation of NLP systems should not only rival human language abilities but also serve as a bridge for diverse communities by providing easy-to-use tools and resources in multiple languages. As a result, there is an increasing need for data efficiency in NLP to make progress towards these goals. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of few-shot learning in NLP, which involves establishing models that can learn from just a small sample size of labeled data across multiple languages. To further advance research in this area, we create the FSLNLP 2022 Dataset, a new evaluation platform that includes six diverse NLP tasks in multiple languages, allowing us to explore the concept of few-shot learning in NLP. Our experiments with this dataset reveal that traditional transfer learning methods are not effective in this setting, whereas models that incorporate additional tasks and utilize the underlying structure of the data exhibit greater efficiency in learning from a small sample size of labeled data. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the feasibility of few-shot learning in NLP, which can empower multilingual communities by providing easy access to NLP tools and enabling the rapid development of models tailored to specific languages and applications. As such, we hope this dataset will serve as a foundation for the advancement of few-shot learning in NLP, which is crucial for the field's continued progress. It is available online at https://fslnlp.org/. It includes six tasks in four languages and can be accessed via the FSLNLP 2022 Challenge website. It has also been integrated into the SuperZero-Base Multilingual NLP Model, which is an open-source repository available on GitHub at https://github.com/leverandera/zmb-mnlp. It is worth highlighting that the goal of this work is to encourage discussion and advance research in this area through the public release of the dataset and the code used in these experiments. It is hoped that this work will contribute to a future discussion on few-shot learning in NLP at a planned workshop to be held in Thirteenth International Conference on Advanced Research in Computer Science (ICAICS 2022). It is also intended as a starting point for the development of new approaches that can be evaluated via the FSLNLP 2022 Challenge. It is anticipated that this challenge will facilitate collaboration among NLP researchers worldwide by providing a common goal and a platform for comparative studies. To accurately calculate the energy loss function of tantalum oxide, a complex system involving spin-orbit coupling and local field effects must be accounted for. This requires combining relativistic density functional theory with the dielectric matrix approach. Our study employs the Herring-Grimmer method to compute interband contributions to the dielectric matrix locally and self-consistently within the exchange-correlation category. To determine the effectiveness of these methods, we conduct two sets of calculations: one with experimental crystallographic data and another with internally consistent theoretical parameters obtained through self-consistent relativistic density functional theory. The findings from both methods reveal similar trends in the energy loss function and allow us to identify distinct energy loss peaks. These results provide a theoretical framework for interpreting experimental data on energy loss spectra of tantalum oxides. Furthermore, we demonstrate the importance of spin-orbit coupling and local field effects in determining the energy loss function through comparative calculations. These effects give rise to significant spectral weight shifts and the formation of additional loss features in tantalum oxide. The computational model we present here can also be applied to other materials exhibiting similar complexities. Human-in-the-Loop (HIL) approaches combine the efficiency of machine learning with critical human oversight, enabling complex models to perform well even with limited data and processing power. A critical component in developing effective HIL systems is determining the most critical annotation tasks. Current methods focus on selecting tasks individually or through a linear process. In contrast, real-world annotation workflows often involve multiple tasks that are highly interconnected, such as classification and bounding box annotation for object detection. To address this complexity, we introduce a novel approach called Constrained Hierarchical Search (CHS), an algorithm that finds the most critical annotation path considering all tasks and their relationships. This algorithm operates within a hierarchical structure, defined by the dependencies between annotation tasks, and incorporates a thorough cost-benefit analysis to evaluate each potential path. The algorithm applies optimization techniques to identify the most critical annotation path, considering both task hierarchy and data distribution, and has been successfully implemented in several real-world applications, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods, delivering up to 21% improvement in annotation efficiency, and effectively leverages the capabilities of machine learning models to prioritize annotation tasks, resulting in a notable improvement of up to 12%. The success of our algorithm has been validated on multiple public datasets, including the PASCAL VOC, MS COCO, and CIFAR, and is now publicly available as a Python package. The CHS algorithm paves the way for the development of more effective HIL systems that can efficiently combine the capabilities of machine learning models with critical human oversight, and is applicable to a broad range of computer vision tasks. Despite the rising popularity of conversational systems, testing them remains a complicated task due to the embedded nature of user input and the lack of a clear specification for desired behavior. Existing automated testing frameworks for these systems fall short, often relying on manual specification writing and limited evaluation metrics. Utilizing knowledge retrieved from massive multilingual datasets has significantly enhanced neural machine translation performance. Nonetheless, the bulk of current research focuses on leveraging knowledge within the same language for machine translation. In contrast, our cross-lingual memory retriever enables a monolingual machine translator to also draw on knowledge from diverse other languages, helping the translator to learn more general and effective representations of language. By incorporating a multi-language knowledge retriever into the neural translator, we observe significant gains in translation accuracy, surpassing traditional bilingual translation memory methods. Moreover, our complete system is highly efficient, requiring no additional training or knowledge bases beyond the underlying machine translator. As a result, the complexity of the system is exceptionally low. We achieve particularly impressive results with a English-to-Spanish machine translator, where we apply this approach with no additional training, gaining +1.3 BLEU points over the traditional method and delivering the current state-of-the-art (42.3 BLEU points) in WMT 2020 robust model evaluation. In addition to this success, our low-complexity cross-lingual memory retriever also raises several thought-provoking questions about the underlying mechanics of machine translation. We also present various ablation studies and a breakthrough where our method surpasses a highly optimized but fundamentally different approach to machine translation. We release our code and data at this link. https://github.com/ghrua/xlm_retriver/tree/main/data/eval_data/LASER_multilingual. Additionally, we include our own detailed analysis of the massive multilingual corpus dataset known as XLM, comprising over 11 billion parameters. In doing so, we delve into the underlying mechanics of machine translation and offer our own theoretical perspective on possible explanations for the success achieved with our cross-lingual memory retriever. In this regard, we observe the diversity of languages used in the training dataset for machine translation has a notable effect on the development of the machine translator's general language understanding. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through comprehensive evaluations conducted on real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing baseline models. Our findings, which were confirmed by MR-only brain and prostate segmentation tasks, indicate that models can achieve high accuracy even when evaluated with unseen MRI data, thanks to the utilization of rich open datasets. This paper formulates network-based multi-agent optimization issues within a general framework that encompasses various specific problems, and proposes a flexible and efficient framework for obtaining high-quality solutions via a decentralized approach. The proposed method, based on the exact characterization of feasible regions, utilizes convex optimization techniques and network flow concepts to achieve this goal. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness by applying it to a particular task - namely, designing an efficient signal routing strategy for multi-agent consensus problems. The method's efficacy is also validated through Monte Carlo simulations, where we compare it to other state-of-the-art methods across a wide range of test cases. To address growing memory demands, programmer access to memory can be directly managed by hardware via direct access memory technologies like NVRAM. Despite offering fast access and moderate capacity, NVRAM requires persistent writes to be managed efficiently to avoid performance degradation due to frequent, small persistent writes. To tackle this issue, a new file system called NOVA-relaxed NVMM is proposed, which works seamlessly with Optane DC PMMs to optimize the NVRAM access experience. NOVA-relaxed NVMM is designed to minimize performance variations caused by small, persistent writes by implementing an optimized logging mechanism. To further enhance performance, NOVA-relaxed NVMM includes an optimized garbage collection technique. Experimental results show noticeable performance improvements in applications prone to small persistent writes, demonstrating the effectiveness of NOVA-relaxed NVMM. Furthermore, an evaluation of various file system configurations reveals that NOVA-relaxed NVMM can achieve substantial performance gains in specific workloads while demonstrating compatibility with existing Linux disk management tools. To facilitate future innovations, the NOVA-relaxed NVMM file system and related components have been open-sourced for developers to explore the possibilities of NVRAM access beyond the scope of this work. As a result, more efficient NVRAM management is now within reach for developers who can leverage NOVA-relaxed NVMM by itself or integrate its components into their own customized NVRAM access solutions. As more direct access memory technologies become available in the future, NOVA-relaxed NVMM is positioned to provide a reliable foundation for developers to tackle the evolving memory demands of contemporary applications. We examined the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ system to understand the effects of Cm on the crystal and magnetic properties. Gd and Cm are both heavy fermion materials with unique magnetic properties, and replacing Cm with Gd allows for the adjustment of the concentration of 5d electrons. Our study discovered that Cm's incorporation induces an enhancement in the magnetic moment, which increases linearly with Cm's composition. Notably, the magnetic moment's change in the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds deviates from the expected ratio of 2+ for heavy electron materials. Additionally, NMR and $\mu$SR measurements provided further insight into the effects of Cm on the electronic and magnetic properties of the system. Our findings suggest that Cm's incorporation induces a transition from an antiferromagnetic state to a paramagnetic state through a spin-lattice relaxation time that becomes increasingly long. The data also imply that the heavy electron state is preserved across the composition range studied. Notably, the increase in magnetic moment is directly proportional to the Cm composition, making the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ system an ideal location to investigate heavy electron state's intersection with ferromagnetism. Upcoming studies will focus on exploring the heavy electron state's intersection with ferromagnetism directly by increasing the Gd composition. Nonetheless, the current results already highlight the significance of the heavy electron state in the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ system and provide a foundation for a more comprehensive investigation of this compelling heavy electron system. Initially, the choice of object detector is treated as a classification problem, with the predictor learning to identify the characteristics of data samples categorized as correctly detected or incorrect. The predicted scores from this classifier are then utilized to weigh the votes of multiple object detectors in a ranking-based model. This study offers a distinctive perspective on estimating the parameters of copulas, a vital aspect of finance, utilizing Bayesian inference. The research introduces a new Bayesian algorithm, the Bayesian Kernel Copula (BKC), based on kernel methods, which can handle various copulas, including their hierarchical forms. Notably, the BKC enables simultaneous parameter estimation for multiple copulas and bridges the gap between autoregressive copulas and their underlying root copula. Theoretical advantages of the BKC include consistency and asymptotic normality for its parameter estimators. Our experiments demonstrate the BKC's effectiveness in comparison to leading alternatives, such as the Inverse Propensity Score (IPS). The BKC's performance particularly excels in tougher scenarios with limited data, a common challenge in financial time series analysis. A concrete application of the BKC is showcased in an analysis of stock price correlations in the Chinese stock market. The BKC's source code is available under the Apache License 2.0 for public use.

Inspired by contemporary network theory, particularly in relation to epidemic spread, we develop a stochastic model where network connections among a population are subject to change. In this model, relationships between any two individuals are modified at designated time points. Specifically, we investigate a scenario where associations between infected and uninfected individuals are terminated, as well as those between recovered and infected individuals. Our analysis focuses on a single generation of the process, where the network evolves according to the described rules. We then determine the expected number of individuals infected at the end of this period. It is shown that the expected number of infections exceeds the initial number, and this expected value can be expressed through a integral involving the generating function of the distribution of connection modification times. Furthermore, intuitive insight into the requirements for connection modification to contribute to the spread of infection is gained through an analysis of the integral's components. We explore the implications of our findings by applying the model to specific stochastic processes. It is demonstrated that, under certain conditions, the expected number of infections at the end of the generation can be represented as the product of the initial number of infections and a coefficient, which depends on the distribution of connection modification times. We also establish that a particular type of distribution, where the right tail decreases at a rate of two, is sufficient to ensure the expected number of infections exceeds the initial number, and provides a upper bound for the expected number of connections modified during one generation. Lastly, we provide an analysis of how our results relate to existing models, such as the Grassmannian model, and discuss possible directions for further research. This paper confirms a conjecture made by Dotti, Hno, and Mazzola in 2019, which links steady Cotton solitons to 3-hyper surface geometry in the context of three-dimensional manifolds. The investigation is expanded to include solitons associated with G$_2$-structures, leading to the discovery that they mirror the geometry of minimal hypersurfaces. The work also demonstrates that both the Cotton soliton and the soliton associated with G$_2$-structures contain a Reeb vector field, either directly or implicitly. If the potential vector field is orthogonal to the Reeb vector field, the steady Cotton soliton is shown to be a gradient soliton with the same potential. This relationship between the solitons and the G$_2$-structure is used to prove that solitons cannot exist in certain manifolds based on the geometry of certain minimal hypersurfaces. A specific example is given where a soliton exists on a manifold that is computable, but this computation does not allow for the calculation of the surface's curvature. Another theoretical soliton is also constructed to show that it is not a surface with a computable curvature. This construction is linked to a specific type of twisted suspension of a certain 2-dimensional manifold. The investigation concludes with the analysis of future research directions in this field. This work was initially presented as separate articles on the solitons associated with 3-hyper surface geometry and those associated with G$_2$-structures in three-dimensional manifolds. Those articles are currently under review for publication. This paper offers a more comprehensive exploration of the relationship between these solitons and the underlying geometry, incorporating new findings and broader implications. A mathematical framework exists that describes how parton distribution functions (PDFs) change under increasing scale transformations known as DGLAP evolution. This study investigates the impact of neglecting higher-order terms when fitting PDFs to data, focusing on a simplified case using a meson distribution and a fit to data from the Drell-Yan process and structure function measurements. Our findings indicate that such an approximation can lead to inaccurate results, with a difference of up to 100% when comparing the PDF at a higher scale, unless the available scale range is sufficiently large to minimize the effect of neglecting higher-order terms. Additionally, this study explores how the choice of renormalization and factorization scales influences the result, with a difference of up to 30% when neglecting next-to-next-to-leading-order terms, and further highlights the importance of incorporating NNLO terms into future PDF fits to ensure accurate results for physical quantities at various scales, especially for scales beyond the current range of available data. As an extension to this study, we provide a set of NNLO PDFs fitted to the data in question, allowing for a more precise calculation of physical quantities such as the inclusive cross-section for top-quark production in hadronic collisions at a scale of $\sim 350$ GeV. This demonstrates that NNLO PDFs can provide more accurate results for physical quantities at scales beyond the range of available data, with a reduction of up to a factor of 10 in the theoretical uncertainty when comparing to NNLO calculations using the MRST2004 NNLO PDFs. This further highlights the importance of incorporating NNLO terms into future PDF fits to ensure accurate results for physical quantities at various scales, especially for scales beyond the current range of available data. This set of NNLO PDFs will be made available through the LHPC repository on the xPDF site. We introduce a variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework for policy evaluation in reinforcement learning, based on an in-depth analysis of how experience replay estimates policy gradients. The framework is versatile and accommodates both direct policy evaluation and offline reinforcement learning as specific cases. By leveraging a batch size that grows polynomially with the number of states, our method achieves a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(d^{2p}H\sqrt{S})$ in direct policy evaluation, where $d$ represents the dimensionality of the action space, $p$ is the degree to which the state values vary relative to the action dimension, and $S$ is the number of states. When applying our framework to offline reinforcement learning, our method achieves a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(d^{2p}H\sqrt{N})$ in the warm-start setting, where $N$ is the number of episodes generated offline, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art for polynomially scaling batch sizes. Our results highlight the potential of experience replay to enhance policy gradient estimation, and our findings are supported by experimental results showing significant improvements under tight batch size constraints. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/yangda-leo/VRER}.

Using high-resolution laser scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, 
we studied the superconducting gap on iron chalcogenide FeTe$_{0.55}$Se$_{0.45}$ 
samples with naturally occurring tear-drop and square hole defects. 
Around the zone corner, a consistent gap of approximately $0.15\epsilon_F$ 
is measured for both defect types, with a rich variation in gap distribution. 
Notably, this gap size is significantly larger than reported for other iron-based 
superconductors, and varies significantly with crystal orientation and alignment. 
We find that tear-drop and square hole defects have distinct crystal and 
electronic structures, with the superconducting gap exhibiting opposite symmetry 
around them. These findings provide a major breakthrough in the understanding of 
defect-induced superconductivity and their relationship with charge density waves. 
They also highlight the unique value of studying superconductivity in relation 
to crystal structure and local electronic states, particularly in the ongoing 
puzzle of resolving the symmetry of the superconducting gap in iron chalcogenides. 
This represents a significant step forward in the ongoing research to clarify 
the fundamental nature of superconductivity in these materials. 
This study demonstrates the capabilities of high-resolution laser scanning 
tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy in investigating the superconducting 
gap structure around atomic-scale defects within the iron chalcogenide 
family, and has significant implications for the field.

Our research focuses on an exclusive measurement within the top quark sector. By analyzing proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, we've developed a method to identify and count events featuring a single top quark that decay into an electron and a muon. From the measured outcomes, we've derived the spin asymmetry of the top quark, which corresponds to 195 picobarns of Lumination with an expected accuracy of plus or minus 0.053. Unprecedented in its kind, this result showcases the minimal discrepancy between data and theoretical standard model predictions. In fact, the difference amounts to a deviation of one standard model error. To further explore the data, we've conducted a comprehensive search for rare top quark decays, examining various branching ratios that reject well-explained standard model scenarios. Although our study falls short of the required sensitivity to detect rare decays as predicted by several popular particle physics theories that extend the standard model, we remain hopeful that future analyses will yield more precise results and help answer fundamental questions about the standard model's fundamental components. Nonetheless, the implementation of this study has a significant contribution to the development of an innovative method for identifying and differentiating between the decay patterns of the $B_c^{\pm}$ meson, which is set to be experimented with in the near future. The introduction of this study has also paved the way for an ongoing investigation aimed at understanding the rare decay of the $B_s$ meson that involves a lepton pair, although the results from these experiments have yet to be factored into the findings reported here. We investigate how the thickness of LaNiO$_3$ layers within superlattices made from LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices affects the temperature-dependent behavior of a rapidly relaxing component in these materials. Our research reveals that these relaxations are influenced by the LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness and display distinct temperature dependencies at higher and lower temperatures. Additionally, we find that the faster relaxing component is linked to the conductivity within the LaNiO$_3$ layers and that this conductivity follows an exponential temperature dependence, which can be described by the activation energy method. The activation energies obtained from this analysis show a clear correlation with the LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness and are influenced by the presence of LaAlO$_3$ layers in a opposite manner at higher and lower temperatures. Our research offers a method for studying the spatial dimensions of a system through the measurement of relaxing components and could provide a framework for examining the temporal dimensions in a similar way. We also propose that the onset of abnormal relaxation at higher temperatures may be related to a shift in the type of magnetic ordering within the LaNiO$_3$ layers. To further understand these findings, we suggest that additional research is needed to uncover the underlying mechanisms governing these results. Our study could have broader implications for our understanding of the conductive properties of complex oxides and may need to be considered in future research. 

This study is significant because it showcases the capabilities of our detection method, which can capture the effects of a system's dimensions on its relaxation behavior. This research could also provide a foundation for investigating temporal dimensions in a way that is analogous to its investigation of spatial dimensions. Additionally, our findings in this study highlight the need for further research into the underlying mechanisms that govern the conductive properties of complex oxides, and any models that are developed as a result of this study could have implications for our understanding of these materials. 

This work is also relevant to the broader field of complex oxides, and it highlights the benefits of combining theoretical and experimental research within this field. Conversational AI systems are becoming increasingly prevalent, and understanding their fundamental components in a cognitive framework is a pressing issue. We argue that two essential concepts, which are closely linked, in this context is the ability to generate dialogue and maintain a sense of mental states, are actually the same - both refer to the capacity to understand other individuals' mental states and generate language accordingly. We reference this combined skill as "conversational mental state understanding" and aim to investigate its structure through a mixed-methods analytical approach, which incorporates both quantitative and qualitative elements in a dialog system's cognitive framework. We begin by examining the theoretical underpinnings of this system through a discussion of both cognitive and computational frameworks, which is then followed by an in-depth review of the underlying linguistic structures necessary for effective dialogue understanding. To further uncover the structure of this system, we design and execute a set of experiments involving both symbolic and connectionist approaches to data-driven state understanding. Our findings from both techniques reveal a crucial discovery, which is that separate modules within the system are capable of simultaneous operation. To provide additional insight into the nature of this system, we also conduct a qualitative analysis through both user evaluations and linguistic analyses of generated text. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of a dual-component system comprising an executive module and a mental state repository, which is further reinforced by the presence of both a context updating mechanism and a retrieval module. With this cognitive framework in place, we believe that we have made significant progress in enhancing our understanding of the underlying psychological elements necessary for effective conversational systems, which in turn, can serve as a foundation for future development in this field. Additionally, many of the cognitive structures we have proposed for conversational systems can also be applied to other generative systems, which is also a topic that is deserving of further exploration. We investigated how protein sequences influence the effect of genetic snips on human traits, even when those snips don't directly affect the protein code. Using a statistical approach that accounts for protein structure and function, we analyzed 480 traits from GWAS and found a significant link between the two factors in nearly a third of them. The effect of the protein sequence on the snips' impact proved significant across all categories of traits and organs they pertain to. Furthermore, by integrating our method with a strategy to identify protein complexes, we found effects linked to those complexes, demonstrating the potential for our approach to contribute to the understanding of GWAS findings and the development of new targets for pharmaceuticals. As an example, we focused on GWAS associated with type 2 diabetes and identified a link between snips affecting the structure of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and diabetes risk. We also discovered that snips with the potential to impact the function of enzymes involved in the glycolytic pathway had a significant effect on their function. Importantly, almost half of the most influential snips in our analysis showed a significant relationship with diabetes development, offering potential applications in the selection of subjects for clinical trials. Additionally, we found that our protocol could reliably replicate the findings made during the initial analysis, assessing the effect of protein sequences on the effect of snips on various traits and organs across GWAS datasets. However, it's essential to thoroughly validate any new approach by replicating results through independent means, such as genetic engineering and functional assays, in order to fully comprehend the biological basis of our discoveries. As a demonstration of this, we focused on GWAS associated with nonsynonomous snips and found evidence supporting the significant link between the effect of protein sequences and snips on these types of genetic variations. By combining our protocol with molecular dynamics simulations, we were also able to provide evidence for the impact of protein sequences on the effect of snips on protein function, such as with aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the value of considering the effect of protein sequences when interpreting the results of GWAS, and paves the way for a deeper understanding of the biological basis of GWAS findings and the development of new targets for pharmaceuticals. In graph theory, adding new vertices to split existing ones is a well-known technique used to simplify complex graphs. Focusing on bipartite graphs, this work explores the effectiveness of this method in achieving planar drawings. A split of a graph $G$ involves replacing a vertex $v$ in $G$ with multiple vertices, while maintaining the same edge connections. We investigate the minimum number of vertex splits required to planarize bipartite graphs in relation to their tubewidth and chordal bipartite graphs in relation to their chordal width. It has been previously proven that some graphs can be planarized with just one vertex split, and that this is also true for all single-source bipartite graphs. Now, we show that for graphs with high tubewidth, a large number of vertex splits is inevitably needed. Furthermore, we find an exact minimum number of vertex splits required for some specific chordal bipartite graphs, and discuss various strategies for dividing vertices. These methods enable us to derive tighter bounds on the number of vertex splits needed for certain families of bipartite graphs. It is demonstrated that splitting vertices can significantly reduce the number of crossings in drawing chordal bipartite graphs. As a result, we are able to planarize certain graphs that cannot be planarized without vertex splits, and we present a verifiable proof for all our findings.

A recent study discovered a critical limitation in the efficacy of Flush+Reload attacks, a sophisticated memory-based side-channel attack, when executing hyper-threading enabled applications. Our research expands upon this discovery, pinpointing the source of the issue to the combination of hyper-threading, cache hierarchies, and the Flush+Reload attack mechanism. We devise a novel HyperDegrade technique capable of mitigating the constraints of cache hierarchies to overcome the limitations of the Flush+Reload attack. By optimizing various cache management strategies, our technique achieves comparable efficacy to the original Flush+Reload attack for non-hyper-threaded applications, requiring only one trace instead of multiple. Furthermore, our HyperDegrade technique provides enhanced time granularity, with options for synchronizing the attacker after every cache kick-out, resulting in significantly reduced attack durations. We validate our technique through a range of cache management experiments and showcase its compatibility with contemporary cache management systems. Despite numerous adaptations and modified versions of this template, assessing its robustness across diverse datasets with varying levels of complexity in heart disease remains a priority. To thoroughly test the template's performance under real-world conditions, we used the MMRR-CMR challenge, which features scans depicting a range of heart diseases. In this study, we evaluated the template's ability to analyze complex cases by applying it to two datasets: a dataset with complex cases (the acicPathological dataset) and one without (the AHA16 dataset). Finally, we analyzed the relationships between segmentation difficulty, dataset complexity, and the template's performance. Notably, we found that the template performed better in segments that were easier to analyze but worse in segments that were harder to analyze. This study explores how small-scale wave propagation affects the larger-scale behavior of a gradient damage model in materials with varying properties. To tackle this issue, we employ dynamic reduction techniques to model the rapid oscillations in a two-scale model. By analyzing the reduced problem, we demonstrate that non-continuous solution paths can arise when there is a significant difference in material properties. However, this phenomenon can be avoided by modifying the model to include an additional gradient term that reflects the average material behavior over a particular scale. Ultimately, our research indicates that higher-order models can be approximated by introducing an additional degree of singularity in the damage variable, which depends on the specific scale in question. This approach enables us to develop a family of effective gradient damage models for brittle materials with varying levels of heterogeneity. To illustrate this, we develop a model with a singular part that follows a specific probability distribution in a two-dimensional analysis. Consequently, this research provides theoretical justification for employing effective gradient damage models in the study of brittle material failure. Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNN) have achieved human-like accuracy in image recognition, yet they are often outperformed by human eyes when identifying large objects in an image. Current DCNN-based object detection approaches typically integrate Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN) to cover objects of differing scales, but their limited base network capacity often hinders performance. To overcome this limitation, we propose an approach where the base network and FPN are optimized jointly with adaptive training strategies to improve base network performance, releasing its full potential when integrated with FPN. By employing three adaptive training strategies, two backbone pre-training methods, and meticulous configuration tuning, we significantly enhance the accuracy of two renowned base networks, achieving a notable increase of +1.1 AP in the COCO validation set. Our approach serves as a comprehensive benchmark, outperforming previous studies and demonstrating that the base network's capacity can be fully unleashed with adaptive training. Moreover, our method empowers the base network to excel in other vision tasks, showcasing its versatility. To facilitate further research, we openly share our adapted code and benchmark models on GitHub. Recent advances in extreme value theory and bivariate conditional modeling have enabled researchers to generate accurate predictions for the tail distribution of a variable, even with limited information. However, existing methods typically require a substantial number of observations, a large value of $n$, to be effective. In contrast, our research offers an alternative approach that allows for extreme value theory tail predictions in scenarios where a limited number of extremely large observations, characterized by a small value of $n$, is available. The new method is based on a specific type of bivariate conditional modeling called the 'factor model'. It reveals that under certain conditions, the tail observations can be represented as a product of two components: a large conditional expectation, given a specific set of standardized variables, and an independently drawn large extreme value, given the same conditions. Consequently, this leads to a useful result where the distribution of the tail, conditional on specific extreme value, predictions can be approximated by the distribution of a specific type of generalized extreme value distribution. It is also shown that this approximation performs well compared to other methods, particularly when a large number of observations, a large value of $m$, is available. Furthermore, our research offers an innovative way to estimate the parameters of this generalized extreme value distribution, even when a small number of extremely large observations, a small value of $m$, is available. It is demonstrated through simulations that these estimated parameters provide an accurate prediction for a new, unseen set of extremely large observations, a small value of $m$. It is also demonstrated that this proposed method outperforms other methods, including the 'heaviest tail' approach, in a real-world application, specifically when analyzing flood frequencies in Germany, as part of the CHASEE project, with data provided by DHM. The methodology developed here is a key contribution to our on-going research project, CHASEE, which aims to provide extreme value theory-based predictions for flood frequencies, in collaboration with German flood risk management authorities. The code related to this research is available at: <https://github.com/Alim16/Extreme-Value-Theory-bivariate-conditioning>. The code used for the simulations, data visualization, and real-world application is also included in this repository. Alternatively, substructures in protoplanetary disks could facilitate planet formation through the accumulation of small particles in designated areas. Despite existing theories, there is a lack of understanding regarding how disk regions can develop and persist as home for developing planets. To address this, we incorporate disk physics into a sophisticated stellar model, and based on stellar observations, we identify how disk processes like gas accretion and turbulence affect the formation of planet-friendly environments. Utilizing these insights, we develop a refined framework for evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution and test it against a range of disk configurations. Our studies reveal how disk features can develop and persist as stable areas, offering a basis for further research into how these environments can facilitate the development of planets. Building upon this foundation, we incorporate additional elements related to planet formation, such as how disk processes can contribute to the formation of planetesimals, and how they can influence the development of planets. Ultimately, our findings underscore the significance of interacting stellar and disk physics in shaping the evolution of planets and their hosts. The BigApple energy density functional, which is a phenomenological density functional used for calculating the properties of nuclear matter, will be comprehensively reevaluated with updated experimental data. This reassessment includes 1865 neutron-rich nuclides, 282 of which have unconfirmed or confidently established magic number statuses. Furthermore, 1214 new reference points with accurately determined masses have been added to the previous study, significantly enhancing the precision of parameter adjustments. The updated analysis reveals a robust consistency of parameters with minimal changes, except for the adjustment of neutron-proton pairing strengths, which was modified to align with the predictions of the shell-model Monte Carlo approach. The revised BigApple functional maintains its strong correlation with various phenomena, such as shell gaps, collective motions, and phase transitions, and accurately predicts the patterns of high-spin states and shape transitions in nuclides like actinides, rare earth regions, and strontium and zirconium isotopes. Notably, the updated functional predicts new candidate magic numbers in the light neutron-rich regions, specifically in the $p$-shell and the $sd$-shell, which could be confirmed by upcoming low-energy mass spectrometry experiments. The BigApple functional provides a unified description of nuclear ground states, collective states, and bound nuclear fragments, setting the stage for predictions on dynamic phenomena and studies of unusual nuclei encountered in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. The revised BigApple functional is now available for public use at the BigApple DFT website. The updated code includes the new parameters and provides calculational tools for nuclear bound states and low-lying collective states. The BigApple DFT can be employed to calculate collective states using the random phase approximation, and it is prepared to handle large-scale calculations with modern high-performance computers. Our study proposes a framework for evaluating the long-term effects of Molmer-Sorensen interactions in ion chains, considering the influence of individual ion motions and lattice vibrations. By analyzing the spectral properties of the Molmer-Sorensen Hamiltonian, we identify two distinct regimes of entanglement generation: a short-duration regime characterized by broad spectral overlap and rapid phase accumulation, and a long-duration regime influenced by frequency dynamics and potential trap decay. Utilizing a laser with a frequency far from resonant Raman transitions can prevent long-duration entanglement formation, while a frequency close to these values can prevent phase accumulation during the duration of the molecular interaction. To illustrate this concept, we calculate the optimal Molmer-Sorensen gate durations for different ion chains and laser frequencies. Our framework is applicable to any Molmer-Sorensen-like gate and provides a practical tool for designing durable, entanglement-generating gates in ion chains. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of considering the influence of individual ion motions and lattice vibrations when employing such gates in long-duration experiments. As a practical application, we propose implementing frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gates, utilizing laser frequencies far from resonant Raman transitions to prevent long-duration entanglement formation, and developing durable, entanglement-generating gates for ion chains. Our research paves the way for a more sophisticated analysis of complex multion operations in ion chains. By extending this framework to account for the influence of spontaneous photon scattering, we can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the interplay between laser-driven entanglement generation and cavity-mediated entanglement distribution in ion chains. This, in turn, will enable the development of robust, multiion protocols for quantum simulation, communication, and computation. As a specific example, we demonstrate the importance of frequency robustness for durable entanglement generation in ion chains consisting of up to 10 ions. Our study sets the stage for a more in-depth analysis of frequency dynamics in ion chains undergoing complex multion operations, leading to the creation of resilient, multiion quantum states essential for large-scale quantum operations. Ultimately, our framework will facilitate a more detailed investigation of the interplay between different phenomena influencing the dynamics of ion chains, such as spontaneous photon scattering, phonon-spectrum structure, and Raman transitions, and a diverse range of applications, including durable multiion protocols for quantum simulation, communication, and computation. Investigating the effects of covalency and size of A and B cations within the perovskite structure, our study examines how volume, A-cation size, and B-cation size influence the degree of B-cation off-centering. Contrary to previous assumptions, our results show that B-cation off-centering are largely determined by the volume and A-cation size rather than B-cation size. Additionally, our findings suggest that B-cation off-centering are directly correlated with volume and negatively with A-cation size. To further understand these relationships, we analyzed the effects of pressure on B-cation off-centering, finding that they increase under high-pressure conditions. Our studies involve a range of simple perovskites (ABO3) and mixed-perovskites (A'B'A"O6) compounds. Through a combination of theoretical and experimental methods, our studies provide valuable insights into the structural properties of perovskites. In particular, our results highlight the significance of considering both A and B cation size when designing perovskite materials with specific B-cation off-centering levels. In the context of harmonic phonons, our findings reveal that volume and A cation size have a more substantial impact on lattice dynamics than B cation size. In the case of filled perovskites (AIII or VA cations), our studies show that B-cation off-centering are correlated with volume and A cation size, and that these relationships hold for both experimental and simulated data. In the context of mixed-perovskites (AIBIIS or VAIIA cations), our results indicate that B-cation off-centering are influenced by both A and B cation size. Through additional analysis of GdFeO3 under high-pressure conditions, our studies demonstrate that B-cation off-centering increase substantially, and that these changes are accompanied by a rotation of B cations and B-O off-centering, and are driven by a combination of volume reduction and electronic changes. In the context of magnetism, our findings show that B-cation off-centering are crucial for determining the magnetic ground state in perovskites, and that both A and B cation size play important roles in this context. Ultimately, our studies provide a comprehensive theoretical and experimental framework for understanding the structural, phononic, and magnetic properties of perovskites, and can be used to design materials with specific B-cation off-centering levels that are critical for unique magnetic properties.

Recent theoretical predictions place GaCu$_3$(OH)$_6$Cl$_2$ as the sole example of a material with Dirac electrons subject to strong gravitational influence, also exhibiting unusual many-body behavior. Investigating this compound's properties, our analysis focuses on whether it can be synthesized in a polymorphically stable form. Through a comprehensive assessment of GaCu$_3$(OH)$_6$Cl$_2$'s structural stability, we identify the need for further experimental study to determine its crystallographic characteristics. Notably, our calculations reveal that the compound's Dirac properties and gravitational responses can be modified through substitution of the Ga$^{3+}$ site with other elements, with stability however depending on the specific substitution. It is found that certain substitutions induce structural transformations with both intramolecular and intermolecular changes, affecting the Dirac bands and gravitational responses in a complex manner. We undertook an in-depth analysis of a Sagnac interferometer's behavior when subject to intense laser pulses, considering the effects of light propagation through various media and the limitations imposed by the speed of light in vacuum. Our review reveals that the usual advantage of the Sagnac interferometer - its insensitivity to back reflection effects - actually only holds when there is no time delay between the incident and returned beams. However, in the case of high-intensity laser pulses, where a significant time difference arises from the Doppler shift induced by the propagating photons, this time delay leads to a profound impact on the behavior of counter-propagating beams. A single face image can generate a range of faces from the same individual based on different face poses, or entirely new faces on unlike poses. In our work, we veer from the standard monolithic approach to face analysis, instead considering a face as the intersection of two surfaces rather than a singular entity. We introduce the Self-aligned Dual Face Regression Network (SADRNet), the first system to reconstruct a face from pose-dependent and pose-independent factors. Our model comprises two surface components with shared and distinct features, using two flexible rotation-aligned sub-nets to capture factor information, and a composite face estimation module to combine the outputs for a unified face shape. By leveraging a rotation-ally invariant operation and aligning sub-nets with face rotation, our system improves rotation-al stability and performance. Experimental results on the large-scale controlled controlled TVUS+MRFFW dataset demonstrate our approach surpasses the state-of-the-art in face analysis and synthesis. Our work paves the way for further research on the geometry of faces, and the capture of non-frontal faces, faces with facial hair, and other complex faces. We also introduce a new dataset, the rotationally varied face video dataset, for the analysis of faces under extreme poses. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/zyhou2021/ SADRNet. The paper also has a supplementary document that can be found at the code website.
