Recent studies utilizing transformation and attention mechanisms in inverse discrete cosine transforms for speech synthesis have demonstrated notable success. This paper delves into a bidirectional attention-based approach that pays close attention to both frequency and time domains, integrating a novel frequency-then-time and time-then-frequency attention model to enhance transformation accuracy. Our proposals are set within the framework of the highly successful WaveNet model. Notably, our experiments yield superior results when measured by objective assessment, outperforming other attention-based methods, and concurrently produce a more natural, human-like speech quality when evaluated subjectively. Additionally, our proposed time-then-frequency attention model achieves comparable performance to other time-domain attention models while utilizing half the number of attention modules, confirming the efficiency of this architecture. Moreover, our proposed frequency-then-time attention model advertises a more efficient use of frequency attention modules, achieving comparable performance to other frequency-domain attention models while utilizing only 75% of the number of attention modules required by them. Consequently, our highly successful bidirectional attention-based Inverse Discrete Cosine Transform remains a highly viable option for further research and development in this domain. The code for our method is available online at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAM-WNIS. The speech samples generated by our method can be found at https://www.speechdata.org/details/441.

The fundamental threat model we've developed, capable of affecting an important system like a Nuclear Power Plant (NPP) through its Non-Restrictive Perimeter (NRP), focuses on the pressure system serving the NPP's containment area. We've identified Flaw Insertion Attacks on the DCS sensors within this system as potentially catastrophic, allowing an adversary to mistakenly believe the containment area has been successfully pressurized. We've explored the feasibility of such attacks on differential pressure sensors (DPSs) and control valves (CVs) within the NRP, revealing that a relatively low-cost attack could potentially cause the release of radioactive materials into the environment. We've also established that the duration and magnitude of this release are directly linked to the number of compromised CPS components. Through the compromise of specific CPS components, we were able to demonstrate the capability to manipulate DCS system data, leading to unsafe operating conditions of the NPP. We've developed a simulation tool that can calculate the impact of these attacks on the NPP's safety, utilizing DCS system data to determine the effectiveness of various attack scenarios. Through our analysis of multiple attack scenarios, we were able to demonstrate the feasibility of these attacks and the critical importance of implementing secure DCS systems within NPPs. Additionally, we propose a novel threat model and a relevant attack model, both of which can be applied to a broader range of industrial pressure systems. We've also established that traditional attack detection methodologies are insufficient for addressing this threat, and instead, we've explored the feasibility of our proposed approach using frequency-based anomaly detection. We plan to further develop and refine this method through additional research. We've conducted an in-depth review of the relevant literature, and our contributions can be summarized as follows: we've developed a novel Flaw Insertion Attack model capable of affecting the safety of an NPP through its NRP, we've established the feasibility of these attacks on DPSs and CVs within the NRP, we've created a simulation tool to calculate the effectiveness of these attacks, we've proposed a frequency-based anomaly detection method, and we've conducted an in-depth review of the underlying threats and existing literature. We intend to build upon these findings through additional research, and we're seeking feedback on our proposed threat model and attack scenarios. We plan to share our simulation tool and frequency-based anomaly detection method with relevant stakeholders in the future. We've already discussed our results with several cybersecurity professionals working with NPPs, and we plan to continue collaborating with them to further refine our approach.

As the transition to a low-carbon economy gathers pace, storage resources are emerging as a crucial component for the effective operation of future energy systems. These resources can optimize performance when driven by risk-averse objectives, but their behavior remains poorly understood at current development stages. Storage units tend to follow similar risk patterns as other generators, but their risk characteristics are difficult to predict and can vary depending on the type of energy storage employed. To address this knowledge gap, we developed a comprehensive dataset utilizing hourly data from 36 European countries for the years 2015 to 2020, which includes a diverse range of 19 different power plants alongside storages such as pumped hydro, batteries, and others. By combining stochastic production forecasts with actual output, we identified the relative risks of storage and generator units within each plant, revealing that the former tends to exhibit higher risk levels due to their limited round-trip efficiencies. However, when integrating storage and generator units within the same plant, the relative risks often shift in favor of the former, likely resulting from optimized operational practices. To further explore these findings, we developed a series of case studies for eight countries, revealing that the behavior of storage resources can vary significantly across different power plants, but often reflects the underlying characteristics of the specific generation technologies employed. The implications of our research for policy-makers are significant, as they suggest that storage resources are capable of optimizing performance when driven by risk-averse objectives. As a result, we propose the use of expected profit as the primary performance metric for storage resources, which can help to better capture the unique risks and rewards associated with these emerging technologies. By operating storage resources in a more decentralized manner, we also anticipate that the full potential of these resources can be better exploited through the implementation of peer-to-peer electricity trading mechanisms. Ultimately, our research provides a theoretical foundation for modeling the behavior of risk-aware storage resources within low-carbon energy systems, which can be further developed through the incorporation of additional data and modeling approaches. This paper presents an innovative adaptive cooperative nonorthogonal multiple access (ACNOMA) protocol that dynamically switches between cooperative and noncooperative modes based on the channel state, effectively mitigating outages. We derive theoretical expressions for the outage probability of ACNOMA in downlink scenarios, and our simulations reveal that ACNOMA achieves a significant reduction in outage probability, with nearly 100% success rate in high signal-to-noise ratio regions, without incurring a substantial increase in complexity. Comparisons with other multiple access protocols, including cooperative orthogonal multiple access, noncooperative NOMA, and SW-NOMA, confirm the superior performance of ACNOMA in terms of outage probability and success rate. Furthermore, our results indicate that ACNOMA can offer successful connections to all users, especially in scenarios with weak base station signals. Additionally, ACNOMA exhibits greater sensitivity to the performance of weak users, resulting in notable gains in success rates for those users. We also propose an efficient acoustic FD-NOMA system that leverages ACNOMA, and demonstrate the potential for this system to support a large number of users in a typical indoor scenario. We also highlight several feasibility aspects of the proposed ACNOMA system, and suggest various research directions for further investigation.

As 5G networks shift towards dynamic TDD, managing time and frequency resources becomes increasingly complex, leading to high latency in reconfiguration. In response, we present an alternative approach, dubbed DREAM, which leverages AI-powered scheduling and power allocation to optimize performance, efficiency, and latency in dynamic TDD systems. Building on an analytical model of TDD bandwidth usage, we frame the problem as a multi-dimensional generalization of the classic offloading problem. To solve this challenge, we develop a method that dynamically generalizes and extends existing solutions to provide efficient scheduling, power allocation, and resource management across all applications, networks, and time dimensions. Evaluations using realistic 5G scenarios and various dynamic TDD configurations demonstrate substantial improvements in performance, energy efficiency, and latency, with support for flexible coexistence between static and dynamic TDD operations. Furthermore, we find that DREAM's performance benefits can be achieved with significantly reduced latency, specifically with an average optimization time of 10 ms or less, and also showcases the system's ability to adapt to rapidly changing network conditions. In addition, DREAM is designed to operate over a wide range of efficiency targets, making it suitable for various use cases and applications. In terms of implementation, we developed a prototype based on OpenAirInterface, allowing us to demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of DREAM with real-world experiments. In conclusion, DREAM represents a pioneering approach to AI-powered scheduling, power allocation, and resource management in dynamic TDD systems, offering substantial performance gains, improved latency, and flexibility. We examine the long-term behavior of solutions to the nonlinear equation $u_t=u_{xx}+f(u)$ on a finite interval, where $f$ has a stable equilibrium at $u=0$. If this equilibrium is uniquely stable, we show that for small data, the solution asymptotically approaches a constant equilibrium state. However, if the equilibrium is unstable at one point, we demonstrate that there are solutions whose values diverge at that point, despite the equilibrium's stability elsewhere. This result is relevant to a particular biological population growth model, where the interval represents a closed region and the point represents a barrier limiting population growth. Unlike the original argument based on a priori estimates, our proof is an example of a prior-free proof. It is an adaptation of an approach recently used to analyze the stability of solitary waves in the full space by L. Rosales and W. Wang.

We demonstrate that this method surpasses the effectiveness of standard K-fold cross validation in providing stable performance metrics and facilitate model selection without incurring substantial computational costs. Moreover, we highlight that the diversity of models produced by J-K-fold cross validation can be leveraged to explore a broader spectrum of machine learning models, as exemplified by our experiments using stochastic gradient boosting models. Deep neural network architectures have reached exceptional performance in various computer vision applications, however, most existing models are highly complex and difficult to deploy in resource-constrained environments. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new approach based on a Teacher-Student architecture, where a lightweight student network is trained to mimic a deep teacher network. By distilling knowledge from the teacher, the student can achieve high performance despite being much lighter. Our method focuses on distributing the student's learning responsibility across multiple teacher network layers, rather than relying on a single global loss function. To achieve this, we develop two novel attention mechanisms to selectively identify key teacher layers and map student layers to corresponding teachers. By combining these attention mechanisms, we achieved outstanding results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, with a significant reduction in the number of parameters in the student network without compromising accuracy. Our method's efficiency is further demonstrated by the ability to deploy a much lighter student model on resource-constrained devices. Our code is openly available at https://github.com/hjdw/TSA.

Bucket Elimination (BE) is a highly efficient algorithm for combining various inference and optimization tasks within flexible, acyclic graphical models. BE's effectiveness stems from its dynamic scoring technique, which allows for the exploration of model subregions by solving smaller, localized problems. However, BE's potential is limited due to its restriction to acyclic models and exact scores. To expand BE's capabilities, we introduce two innovations. Firstly, we include a procedure to eliminate non-binary variables, which enables the full potential of modern constraint solvers to be leveraged. Secondly, we develop a method for dynamically incorporating approximate score functions, which can be learned from a large dataset. The resulting algorithm, BE-DL, maintains BE's efficient domain-reduction property while incorporating the strengths of deep learning and graphical models. We demonstrate BE-DL's effectiveness by showing that it outperforms BE and other state-of-the-art methods on several real-world datasets. The source code for BE-DL is openly available, and we include experiments that showcase BE-DL's performance along with comparative studies between the different implementations. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications and showcase a real-world scenario involving an airline's flight scheduling problem. The pilot's working hours are governed by complex regulations, which BE-DL effectively learns to capture using a deep learning approach, surpassing traditional constraint-solver-based methods. Given the current lack of fundamental theory, we choose a simplified strong dynamics scenario to evaluate the particle production within the available energy range, also considering the influence of new physics on the existing particle population and the collider's system limitations. Our study involves both pair production and scattering processes, accounting for inherent QCD effects, as well as the dependence on squark properties, collider parameters, and the finite muon lifetime. To facilitate easy integration with future theoretical models, we provide the accessible parameter space in the form of predictions for various cross-section and distribution patterns. By comparing the pair production of squarks and the di-tau scattering processes, or vector boson scattering, we illustrate the potential for the collider to distinguish between different scenarios and theories through measurement of different process cross-sections. Additionally, our analysis highlights the importance of incorporating the finite muon lifetime and the effects of muon system finite detector acceptance in such theoretical predictions. The developed framework is also applicable to studies of other new physics scenarios within the available energy range. As an independent consideration, we find that a 1-TeV 14-TeV muon collider, equipped with a suitable muon recirculation architecture, could provide for pair production of top squarks at acceptable cross-section levels, despite previous calculations indicating this might be achievable only with a 33-TeV operating energy. The outcome of this study is complementary to, and independent of, the ongoing design optimizations of the future muon collider facilities. The specific case considerations discussed here can be examined with additional theoretical scenarios, where such analysis could contribute to the ongoing design process of the future muon collider facilities. The associated code for the studies reported in this work is available online at this link. 

This work is further being developed into a comprehensive theoretical scenario, which will be presented in a follow-up report. That report will explore the potential for the collider to detect the fully integrated new physics scenario, involving the entire spectrum of the fundamental particle population, assuming its operating energy and luminosity. Until then, the framework presented here can be used by the theoretical community to independently evaluate the pair production and scattering processes, or incorporate the finite muon lifetime and the effects of the muon system finite detector acceptance in such theoretical predictions. This research paper extends the scope of applications for control barrier functions (CBFs) by incorporating an alternative framework known as ICCBFs, which encompasses a higher-order CBF framework. The ICCBF framework is equivalent to higher-order control barrier functions (HOCBFs) and is applicable to systems that can be represented by control Lyapunov functions (CLFs). A key advantage of the ICCBF framework is its ability to handle systems with non-continuous jumps in state changes. A specific case study involving a quadrotor aircraft is used to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed ICCBF framework. The study first establishes that a controller utilizing an ICCBF can generate a control input that drives the system states towards the desired target set. The feasibility of the proposed control approach is then validated through real-world flights on a quadrotor aircraft, along with the effectiveness of the ICCBF framework in achieving the desired target set. The proposed framework also facilitates a theoretical contribution to systems governed by CLFs and showcases the ICCBF's equivalence to HOCBFs. The study highlights the importance of distinctness between CLFs and CBFs in its quadrotor case study. The results show that the quadrotor aircraft controls generated by the ICCBF framework are comparable to those obtained from HOCBFs, despite the systems being feasible under CLFs. The study also highlights the advantages of using HOCBFs over CLFs in systems with nominal state stability, as it can lead to more efficient convergence rates in systems. The work presented is a foundation for further research on the ICCBF framework, especially in systems with dynamic CBFs and nonlinear systems with nominal state stability. The study is accompanied by its code, which is publicly accessible for replication purposes. This study examines how the collapse of shipping cartels affected freight rates and shipping volume from 1945 to the present, with a focus on the pre-neoliberal and neoliberal eras. To conduct the analysis, a differential game model was employed, with separate sections addressing the pre-neoliberal and neoliberal periods. Unfortunately, available data for the modern era is too limited, but plausible scenarios for the most recent period can still be assessed. Our research finds that in the pre-neoliberal era, freight rates were significantly inflated due to the cartels' price-setting power, but this led to an increase in shipping volumes as shipowners took advantage of the overpriced markets. In contrast, the neoliberal era saw a reduction in freight rates and shipping volumes as the broken cartels gave way to chaotic, low-cost shipping. For the most recent period, plausible scenarios suggest that freight rates have continued to drop and shipping volumes have risen in response to declining costs. Overall, our analysis suggests that freight rates and shipping volumes have continued to decline at an even faster rate since the cartels broke down. This is consistent with the empirical observations discussed in the introductory chapter. Finally, we explore the implications of our model for the understanding of shipping cartels and the effects of neolibralism in the industry. According to the model, the benefits of breaking up the cartels are greatest when shipping volumes are high, and the greater efficiency of shipping in the neoliberal era is primarily driven by the reduced costs of shipping, rather than any fundamental change in the structure of the industry. Additionally, the study finds that the shipowners' ability to profit from frequent sailings is a key factor in the continued decline of freight rates and shipping volumes. The model also highlights the importance of distinguishing between the pre-neoliberal and neoliberal eras, as the two periods have different dynamics despite sharing a common feature of broken cartels. The model is validated through inductive reasoning, and the results for the most recent period are interpreted as suggesting that the industry has continued to move towards the neoliberal equilibrium predicted by the model. The study contributes to the existing literature on shipping cartels through the development of a game theory model that explains the effects of neolibralism in the industry, and provides a framework for analyzing the breakdown of shipping cartels that can be applied to other situations. The model is flexible and can be adapted to address a broad range of questions about the industry, and the research is accompanied by data that highlights the ongoing decline of freight rates and shipping volumes in the post-cartel era. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have consistently demonstrated superiority over traditional deep learning techniques in processing complex data structured as graphs. Researchers attribute the efficacy of GNNs primarily to the structural aspects of graphs, challenging the conventional assumption that raw node features are essential for accurate predictions. This study seeks to investigate the relative importance of graph structure and node features in GNNs by conducting a comprehensive experiment across multiple datasets and scenarios. We found that graph structure has a limited impact compared to node features, which is counterintuitive given the prominent role assigned to structure in GNN theories. To further illustrate this discrepancy, we developed a simple prototype using a prototype search space, where a graph based on this prototype consistently performed worse than one based on node features. This finding encourages future research to explore ways to incorporate structure information more effectively, perhaps by leveraging flexible graph representations that adapt to node features dynamically. Our study has significant implications for the community, suggesting that GNNs can be equivalently modeled using node features alone and raising questions about the validity of models that rely heavily on graph structures. To facilitate replication and further investigation, we have made our experiment dataset and protocol publicly available. Our study paves the way for a deeper reevaluation of GNN architectures and graph-based models, prompting considerations about the inherent value of graph structures in machine learning. In particular, our work challenges the practice of incorporating structure information through node feature transformations, emphasizing the need to explore more direct ways to incorporate structure. We hope our study will spark theoretical and empirical research into the effectiveness of graph structures in GNNs, enabling a more precise understanding of the complex interplay between graph structure and node features. This understanding is critical for the design and development of more effective GNN architectures that leverage both structure and node features in a synergistic manner. As a starting point, we propose a basic framework consisting of multiple parallel subnetworks, each focused on a node's feature and neighboring structure. Each subnetwork takes the node's feature and its adjacent graph as input, producing a representation that is combined to generate the final node representation. We also conducted a prototype search within this framework, experimenting with diverse receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves as the objective function. Our results demonstrated that graph structure has a limited contribution compared to node features, which prompted us to explore ways to incorporate structure information more effectively. We believe our study has significant implications for the community, encouraging a reevaluation of GNN architectures and graph-based models, as well as a deeper consideration of the complex interplay between graph structure and node features

This paper investigates compact, singular areas within a higher-dimensional Euclidean space that minimize volume among sets bounded by surfaces of constant curvature. We specifically examine "double cone" types of singularities found in positive scalar curvature areas and provide a detailed analysis of their associated geometry. Through a process of surgery, we can understand the structure of these areas by removing and reassembling such singularities at higher levels of resolution. Our analysis of the geometry surrounding a double cone-type singularity enables us to establish the existence of compact, singular areas with minimal volume and bounded by surfaces of constant curvature, without any restriction on the scalar curvature within a specific regime of positive values. This existence result is demonstrated through a strategic combination of surgery style arguments and the Regge functional approach, allowing us to overcome obstacles posed by low-resolution structures of the set. The outcome of this analysis reveals that for a particular set of outer angles, there exist compact, singular areas with minimal volume and positive scalar curvature within a specified volume range. This development builds upon previous work by Shoen, where sets with minimal volume and constant positive scalar curvature were constructed using surgery within a particular volume range. However, this new contribution expands upon that result by removing the limitation on set curvature and establishing the existence of analogous sets within a wider volume range. The proposed compact, singular areas also provide a corresponding lower bound for a related energy functional, the Jacobi angular energy. The relationship between this energy and the sets it pertains to is analyzed through a family of "cut sets" that can either increase or decrease the energy based on the angles involved. The outcome of this investigation, where sets with particular angles are considered, leads to a more precise understanding of how the Jacobi angular energy is related to the volume of the set, especially in the vicinity of a double cone-type singularity. The entropy within a vortex core in superconductors is found to be significantly lower than the entropy associated with a moving magnetic flux line, contradicting the assumption that entropy rates are equal at corresponding points. By drawing a comparison to moving magnetic flux lines, the paper determines the entropy within a vortex core, specifically in the $A$-phase of cuprates, and finds it to be proportionally similar to the entropy of a moving magnetic flux line in a normal metal. The discrepancy arises from the unique properties of a vortex core, which cannot be understood through the conventional mapping of heat transport to electromagnetic mapping, and instead, the relationship between entropy and flux line velocity needs to be considered as a coupled electromagnetic-thermal phenomenon. The proportionality between core entropy and flux line energy is demonstrated, and the coefficient is found to be the vortex specific-heat capacity, which is a key physical parameter that has yet to be explored in depth. The vortex specific-heat capacity is further shown to be an important factor in determining the thermal relaxation time of a vortex core. The underlying principles of these relationships are then applied to explain recent experimental findings involving thermal relaxation in vortex cores. The vortex specific-heat capacity is distinguished from the total specific-heat capacity of a vortex core, and a proposal is made to experimentally measure these components separately. The proposed experimental approach involves creating a vortex array and studying thermal relaxation in the presence of an external magnetic field, which would provide valuable insights into the total specific-heat capacity, vortex specific-heat capacity, and the heating of the vortex line itself. The proposed experimental approach would offer a comprehensive understanding of the thermal properties of vortex cores and could potentially facilitate the development of more effective thermal management strategies in superconducting materials. Quantitative analysis in stock market prediction often relies on technical indicators and historical price data. Despite the value of this information, the stocks' actual future behavior remains uncertain. In our research, we utilized a financial database, fine-tuned a linear regression model, and evaluated the performance of multiple technical indicators from the perspective of the stocks they were generated from. Our results demonstrated that the model's accuracy increased with more technical indicators, yet also highlighted the issue of feature collinearity. We addressed this challenge through principal component analysis (PCA), applying it to the indicators before linear regression. Our findings showed that by reducing data dimensions with PCA, the model's accuracy actually decreased, suggesting that the presence of certain factors (likely noise) in the stocks' future behavior is inhibiting the model's effectiveness. This is consistent with the idea that the stock market is inherently difficult to predict due to the presence of noise in price movements. In this context, the value lies in identifying the relevant underlying factors, regardless of the presence of noise in the data. This approach enabled us to develop a linear regression model that could accurately predict stock performance, achieving a high R-squared value of 0.83. However, when testing this model on an unrelated stock, the result was significantly less effective, highlighting the challenge of applying theoretical models to real-world predictions. In the case of stock movement prediction, a more promising strategy may involve incorporating technical indicators and historical price data within more advanced algorithms, such as neural networks, that can handle the complexities and uncertainties of the stock market. This could potentially lead to the development of increased accuracy models capable of predicting stock behavior when tested with new data. In this research, we did not pursue this pathway, instead focusing on the application of linear regression and PCA to better understand the interplay between technical indicators, stock prices, and the presence of noise in price movements. Nevertheless, our study provides a foundation for more comprehensive investigations into the prediction of stock market behavior. The vast majority of massive star mergers are thought to result from white dwarf collisions, which can also produce a supernova explosion. However, few studies have examined the effects of such a event on the surrounding environment, specifically how binary combinations of white dwarfs interact with their neighbors under various mass conditions. This paper explores various WD mergers, including direct collisions, mergers with compact objects, and interactions with neutron stars or black holes, as well as scenarios where a WD is engulfed by a expanding white dwarf. Using a combination of numerical integration and approximate analytical models, we simulated these events and tracked the motion of nearby stars. Our findings indicate that when a WD collides with a compact object, it may generate a massive compact object if it sheds its outer layers, whereas in cases where a WD is engulfed by another expanding WD, it may result in a highly eccentric orbit. Our research reveals that only direct WD collisions have a significant impact on neighboring stars, causing them to be ejected from the potential well of the merging WD. This may lead to a detection of rare, binary WD systems with significant orbital eccentricity resulting from a major merger event. Furthermore, we propose that future surveys should prioritize the examination of rare, ejected star candidates during WD collision detection efforts. These candidates, which could take the form of hot subdwarfs, may offer valuable insights into the behavior of WD binaries and the spectrum of WD collision outcomes. Lastly, we estimate that, given the current number of known WD binaries, there may be around 10-100 candidate ejected stars waiting to be discovered. Contrary to earlier findings, our results show that the drag experienced by the intruder does not follow a clear relationship with the properties of the granular material; instead, we observe a more complex phenomenon in which the drag varies significantly with the driving rate and intruder velocity. To better understand this behavior, we propose a theoretical model that combines elements of quasi-static frictional forces and velocity-dependent dissipation. By applying this model, we are able to successfully reproduce the observed drag characteristics across a range of driving rates and intruder velocities. Our analysis suggests that at low driving rates, the drag behaves in a manner consistent with static friction, but as the driving rate increases, the drag shifts toward a velocity-dependent behavior influenced by frictional dissipation. This transition occurs when the intruder velocity becomes comparable to its own vibration and a significant fraction of the granular bed's vibration. Our study provides a theoretical framework for explaining the drag characteristics of intruders moving through granular materials and offers a set of parameters that can be applied to a broader range of situations. Furthermore, we propose that this behavior could be a manifestation of a first-order phase transition in the intruder's motion, where the drag experienced is a result of the intruder being "trapped" in a quasi-static state within the granular material. Finding optimal configuration combinations that meet complex requirements in large, multi-dimensional spaces has been a challenging problem. This challenge is further compounded by the need to obtain configuration values automatically, without human intervention. Currently, existing configuration retrieval approaches typically rely on static queries that are applied to individual configurations, resulting in a time-consuming process to identify efficient configuration combinations. In contrast, we introduce BoAnon, an innovative framework that allows us to derive a formal description of desired configuration specifications and perform efficient query optimization. By leveraging relational algebra and a novel indexing mechanism known as the selection index, BoAnon enables the automatic discovery of effective configuration combinations. This is achieved through a single, streamlined query that produces a comprehensive set of required configurations. Furthermore, BoAnon facilitates dynamic configuration evolution, enabling us to adapt existing configurations to meet evolving requirements. Extensive benchmarking experiments have validated the exceptional performance and flexibility of BoAnon, with our framework yielding superior results when compared to both traditional configuration retrieval methods and state-of-the-art configuration optimization tools. Additionally, we have applied BoAnon successfully in real-world settings, with notable deployments in large-scale distributed systems and cloud computing environments. BoAnon is now available as an open-source project on GitHub.

Therefore, interpreting observations and attempting to draw inferences about the working of the active galaxy's central engine is highly  dependent on shock dynamics. Nevertheless, by studying the evolution of shocks  in power sources like quasars and radio galaxies, researchers can gain valuable  insights into how matter and energy interact in these systems. The research presented here is the starting point for a much  more comprehensive study of shock dynamics in active galaxies, which will be  carried out in future works by examining potential pairs of active galaxies and  analyzing data from various astrophysical radiation fields. This paper is part of  a larger project that aims to study the working of active galaxies in their own  right, as well as to use shock-ionization as a tool to gain a deeper  understanding of how these power sources relate to their surrounding environments. We demonstrate that a Cayley tree, which serves as the framework for the Ising model, can be interpreted through the lens of group theory. By examining the rotational group SO(2N), we can divide it into two equivalent series: one comprised of representations associated with the Ising model on a Cayley tree, and another comprising the Dirac fermion's representations in a lattice based on the hypercubic structure. This mathematical framework allows us to employ the principles of group representation to derive exact correlation functions for the Ising model on a Cayley tree using the coordinate Bethe ansatz. Furthermore, we propose the application of this method to study the Ising model with long-range interactions and relate it to a specific quantum system known as the XXZ Heisenberg chain with alternating spins. By doing so, we anticipate gaining insight into the spectral structure of these systems. To support our proposal, we calculate the correlation lengths of the Ising model and the XXZ chain with alternating spins by employing the coordinate Bethe ansatz. Additionally, we investigate how the correlation lengths change with the spin anisotropy parameter Δ. Lastly, we discuss the potential to use this representation-based approach to analyze other lattice systems in a Cayley tree structure.

To this end, we establish a significant result regarding the ergodicity of systems in high-dimensional spaces, building on previous work by Ferrer and Karafyllis, who investigated the ergodicity of systems in two-dimensional spaces. Specifically, we demonstrate that if a system defined by a vector field is ergodic in a subset of a higher-dimensional space, it is also ergodic in the entire space. Moreover, we show that this ergodicity property holds not just for the full shift, but also for any factor of the full shift. This result is an explicit contribution to addressing the Joint Ergodicity Conjecture. Concerning the Orbits Principle Conjecture, we prove that any system whose orbits are uniformly distributed under a given measure, can be ergodic with respect to that measure. This is implicit in our previous result. We incorporate supernovae and stellar winds into a hydrodynamic model of superbubbles within massive molecular clouds, addressing their effects on pair-instability and core-collapse SNe as well as the cooling of gas. By simulating various scenarios, we reveal that pair-instability and core-collapse SNe, in addition to core collapse contributing to heavy elements, also significantly enhance dust production through the fragmentation of massive stars and the destruction of dust by pair-instability SNe. This increased dust amount, resulting from the additional heavy elements produced within superbubbles, can lead to significant dust formation through the cooling and cooling-driven fragmentation of ejected gas. As a consequence, the total dust produced within superbubbles becomes a major contributor to the overall dust budget within these massive molecular clouds. Observational evidence, specifically the abundance of silicon and the presence of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon features within superbubbles, can serve as indicators of the additional heavy elements produced through pair-instability and core-collapse SNe within these regions. Furthermore, the presence of dust within superbubbles may also provide a distinguishing characteristic for identifying pair-instability SNe, given the difficulty in detecting these events directly. To address the challenge of 3D object detection in far-field scenarios, we propose a dual-detection framework that combines RGB and lidar-based approaches. Our framework utilizes both end-to-end neural network methods for RGB-image-based detection and traditional lidar-point-cloud-based detection. The fusion process is achieved by concatenating the detected bounding box coordinates from both domains, with subsequent refinement through a classifier and pruner. We evaluate our approach on the Waymo Open Dataset, and our results demonstrate improved performance compared to standard 3D detection methods. Our code is openly available at https://github.com/CrazyDogTeam/DualDetection.

While self-supervised flow estimation has achieved significant progress, there remains a crucial aspect to address: occlusions. Our research aims to mitigate this limitation by introducing a novel method, Uncovering Hidden Motions (UHM), which utilizes a reciprocal prediction mechanism. UHM incorporates a unique, bidirectional learning strategy that enables the use of both forward and reverse flows. By incorporating a reciprocal prediction mechanism, we're able to uncover hidden motions and accurately estimate flows through occlusions. Our evaluation using the MT2100 graphics card on the ADE20K dataset reveals that our method outperforms current self-supervised flow estimation models and demonstrates robust performance in occluded areas. Furthermore, UHM showcases superior performance on the KITTI dataset when optimized on the ADE20K dataset, highlighting its potential for practical applications. Our code and dataset have been made available at https://github.com/cg1177/UHM.

This paper introduces a novel technique called Timeloops, which enables the optional omission of system calls in certain software programs. Unlike other methods, Timeloops is unique in that it is designed to work with programs written in interpreted languages, such as PHP and Python. The system incorporates a specialized system call wrapper that is responsible for managing the system calls made by the application. When an application makes a system call, the wrapper checks if the call can be skipped according to the specified time-based rules. If the system call is deemed unnecessary, the wrapper uses a technique called transactional patching to temporarily reverse the effects of the system call when the original time period is reached. The system was successfully tested on real-world programs written in Python, showing that it can effectively eliminate system calls without causing data corruption. Furthermore, the system's performance can be optimized to minimize the overhead of system call omission. The study also explores the potential limitations of Timeloops, such as its inability to handle system calls with persistent effects and those that involve interacting with other system components. The evaluation indicates that the system call wrapper's overhead is minimal, amounting to approximately 100-500 nanoseconds, and that the most significant contributors to this overhead are the operating system's system call overhead and the application's own processing time. The study demonstrates that Timeloops can safely eliminate system calls with a success rate of over 90%, and the results highlight opportunities for further optimization and system call set management. The paper's contributions are twofold, offering a system call filtering technique compatible with interpreted languages and providing a means of managing system calls based on time. The study's findings can inform the development of applications with adaptive system call behavior. The paper's techniques can also be adapted for use in other memory management contexts, such as virtual machines, and presents a system call filtering framework that is open to extension with additional policies and strategies. The paper's techniques have been made available as an open-source implementation, along with a Python-based system call wrapper that enables system call omission and provides the operating system's system call interface as a set of configurable components. In DED2D systems, the TFIET (Time-Fixed Island Energy Transfer) scheme is an alternative to TFE (Time-Fixed Energy Transfer). The TFE scheme divides time into equal energy transfer intervals, where users can receive data and energy simultaneously, or individually in separate time slots. In contrast, the TFIET scheme splits time into "islands," where users can get data and energy transferred during one island, or delay to another island. We studied the TFIET scheme's sum rate and energy harvesting rate performance under the assumption of full DED2D base station connectivity. By analyzing the system's characteristics, we categorized the TFIET scheme as a special case of iterative worst-case decoding, where the sender transmits messages after considering the receiver's potential next island. We derived the optimal TFIET scheme, as well as its statistical performance, by treating the system's parameters as independent and identically distributed. We also established the connection between TFIET and TFE schemes, presenting the TFE scheme as a special case of the TFIET scheme with infinitely small islands. We conducted numerical simulations to validate our analytical findings. The results show that the TFIET scheme outperforms the TFE scheme in terms of rate performance, but may lead to slower convergence. The TFIET scheme's performance depends on the size of the islands, and offers potential harvestable energy gains under certain conditions. The effectiveness of electrostatic phase plates (EPPs) is crucial in scanning transmission electron microscopes and varies significantly based on the design of these plates, specifically how much of each pixel is occupied by electrons as they exit the plate. This study thoroughly examines the optimal design of EPPs to achieve the smallest possible electron probe size and highest current density. We analyzed various design parameters, including fill-factor, pixel pattern, and shape, as well as the relationship between these factors and probe performance. Our results demonstrate that to maximize current density, the area under the electron dose distribution in the direction perpendicular to the beam direction should be minimized, which can be achieved by reducing the fill-factor. Conversely, probe size is optimized by increasing the fill-factor, specifically by distributing electrons across multiple pixels in the beam direction. Based on these findings, we propose a method for manufacturing EPPs with optimized patterns, using a technique that combines electron back-flow imaging and local dose adjustment through the use of EPPs with varied fill-factors and shapes. This method allows for real-time probe characterization and EPP optimization, enabling faster development of high-performance electron probes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by manufacturing a probe with an optimized pattern, featuring a 0.3 Angstrom diameter and current density of approximately 50 A/angstrom^2. This study provides a theoretical foundation for the development of advanced EPP designs, enabling the creation of electron probes with optimized sizes and current densities for various electron microscopy applications. Furthermore, our results highlight the potential of this field to contribute to the improvement of transmission electron microscope performance. Understanding how the complex structure of a developed retina, specifically the spatial distribution of nerve cells within it, evolves from a retinal precursor population is crucial. Retinal precursor cells migrate randomly and systematically to their ultimate positions during retinogenesis. Although previous research has examined individual precursor cell migrations, a comprehensive analysis across all retinal precursors has only been theoretically predicted through simplified models. Our study utilizes high-resolution data of nuclear distributions across the entire zebrafish retina at various stages and a novel statistical approach to evaluate the spatial clustering of retinal precursors. By comparing these findings to simulations of the retinal precursor migration process, we can determine the key factors influencing nuclear distribution across the retina and the retinogenesis process. Our data indicate that the initial retinal precursor clustering dissipates as cells enter the late stages of migration, and that nuclear positions across the retina are determined by a dynamic balance between retinal precursor migration and cell elimination through programmed cell death. Notably, the distribution of nuclei within specific non-overlapping retinal areas is nearly uniformly random, whereas the distribution of nuclei across the entire retina is characterized by evident clustering and spatial patterning. Our study provides a comprehensive analysis of the retinal precursor migration process and the resulting nucleus distribution across the retina and can serve as a reference model for the study of other complex tissue development processes. Through the integration of experimental data and mathematical simulations, our work is a prime example of the value of an integrated approach to the study of complex biological systems and phenomena. Our study's findings are equally relevant to the broader field of collective cell migration and the underlying mechanisms giving rise to the intricate patterns observed in development and tissue homeostasis. Furthermore, our work offers a comprehensive framework for the analysis of cell migration patterns and the evaluation of theoretical models of this process, and can serve as a foundation for a deeper exploration of the fundamental biophysical principles governing cell movement and force generation during individual cell migrations. Through this integrated approach, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the intricate dance of cells migrating collectively to their ultimate positions across complex tissues. Our study specifically examines the evolution of the retinal nucleus distribution across the retina and the retinogenesis process as a whole, and our findings can serve as a reference model for the development and homeostasis of other tissues and organs. We investigate the long-term behavior of active particles within two dimensions using a pair-shape biasing method, which allows us to create detailed simulations for up to 10,000 particles. By comparing our findings to hydrodynamical models, we determine that for dimensions between 2 and 5, active particles exhibit a distinct scaling that differs from linearized hydrodynamics, with correlations diminishing at a rate of $1 \sim 2$ instead of the predicted $1$ in these dimensions. Our simulations also demonstrate that for two dimensions, fluctuations follow a specific pattern, closely mimicking those seen in the Nordström model, and that for dimensions above two, active particles demonstrate a different type of motion, characterized by circular movements that increase in speed with the number of particles, with correlations playing a significant role in this behavior. We further find that despite varying dimensions, the relationship between the motion of individual particles and the collective behavior of the system remains consistent, with particles moving in the opposite direction of their previous steps contributing the most to circular movements. This opposing movement effect becomes more pronounced in higher dimensions, where particles have more room to move freely. We also offer a theoretical explanation for these observations, offering a more in-depth analysis of active motion that considers the interactions between particles and proposes a heuristic model to calculate the circular movement effect. This study provides meaningful insights into our understanding of active systems, offering predictions that can be tested with more advanced simulations, and is available online at <https://github.com/haofeng-wang/2D-active-particles>. Determining whether a set of rational functions in one variable is continuous can be challenging, as it involves evaluating limits that may extend to infinity. However, we demonstrate that using finite sequences, we can assess the long-term behavior of these limits through a computational procedure based on polynomial operations and finite sequence manipulations, in a way that is efficient (specifically, NP-comparable) when the functions have continuous intervals and no infinite limits. If the functions have infinite limits at certain points, determining their long-term behavior requires an infinite number of calculations and, in this case, the functions' continuity can be determined using a computational procedure that explores all possible finite sequences and is based on a combination of polynomial operations and modular arithmetic, with a computational complexity of NP-complete. Additionally, we decide the feasibility of these procedures for various types of complex functions, including those with infinite limits at discrete points, infinite limits at continuous points, and continuous intervals with no infinite limits. We also consider the implications of our results for complex functions of multiple variables. We note that our procedures provide decision-making tools for evaluating the continuity of complex functions through computational exploration of finite sequences, and are distinct from other methods that use analytic or geometric approaches. We offer our algorithms as a novel contribution to the study of complex functions and computational complexity, and suggest they may be of interest to researchers in both fields. We're exploring an alternative approach, where a reservoir is trained to replicate the dynamics of a system using only a time-series of its output data. We'll examine two examples: the first involves using a reservoir to generate multiple co-existing states in a simple optical map system, while the second example involves speeding up a system with slow time scales in a Chua circuit using a reservoir. Both experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this method in complex systems. We also discuss the potential applications and challenges associated with this approach. Furthermore, we highlight how this technique could be adapted for other machine learning systems, such as neural networks. This paper investigates the problem of estimating the state of an autonomous vehicle using feedback control to determine the reachable state set within a given time frame. By continuously disseminating state estimates and control inputs, we can gradually shrink the state uncertainty set. We represent the dynamic system using a control-Lyapunov function, which allows us to derive a finite time state uncertainty set. The standard quadratic regulator is used as an example to demonstrate the procedure, resulting in an optimal feedback controller that reduces the uncertainty set exponentially. Furthermore, we demonstrate that feeding back the state estimate via a sensor with measurement noise adds a bound to the uncertainty set, but this bound can be tightened (though not minimized) for an ideal sensor. The resulting state uncertainty set dimensions can be controlled through the choice of feedback gain, which leads to a suboptimal solution that achieves exponential decay of the uncertainty set dimensions. To compensate for external system disturbances, an additional bound is added to the state uncertainty set, and we can increase the feedback gain to tighten this bound as well. Consequently, we can design the feedback controller to achieve any desired exponential decay rate of the uncertainty set dimensions, regardless of the sensor noise characteristics. The state uncertainty set bounds can be adjusted through the choice of reference trajectory velocity, which is determined by the solution to a nonlinear optimization problem. Ultimately, the finite-time state uncertainty set dimensions can be controlled through the choice of feedback gain, and we can increase the gain to achieve any desired exponential decay rate of the uncertainty set dimensions, which holds even in the presence of external system disturbances and sensor measurement noise. As a result, the state uncertainty set can be reduced to any desired dimension, which provides a computationally efficient method for estimating the state of an autonomous vehicle using feedback control. We constructed two tasks for the Michelson Dataset, one assessing categorizability and the other agency, with 13 animacy dimensions. Categorizability plays a larger role in the hierarchy of supercategories, while agency is more significant in the hierarchy of subcategories. Additionally, our results indicate that categorizability and agency share a common base but also exhibit distinct patterns in distribution. We compare our approach to two alternative methods, both based on hierarchical structures, and find that our continuous scale-based method yields more accurate results. This codiskcyclicity criterion is simplified to a condition on the operator semigroup itself, leading to a more manageable test for codiskcyclicity. Furthermore, conditions are derived to codiskcyclic operator semigroups whose generator has a codiskcyclic extension, influencing the codiskcyclicity of original subgenerators within these extended operator semigroups. These results are applied to a specific integral operator semigroup $\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{h}$ on the space $\mathfrak{X}_\mathfrak{h}$, yielding its codiskcyclicity whenever the function $\mathfrak{h}$ satisfies a specific inequality. This codiskcyclicity of $\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{h}$ enables proof of the density of a set on the disk $\mathfrak{D}$, related to a problem formulated by Arendt and Warma. Additionally, this codiskcyclicity of $\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{h}$ leads to the codiskcyclicity of its original subgenerators $\mathfrak{A}^\mathfrak{h}_0$ and $\mathfrak{A}^\mathfrak{h}_1$. This codiskcyclicity of $\mathfrak{A}^\mathfrak{h}_0$ implies the density of a set on the disk $\mathfrak{D}$, solving the aforementioned problem of Arendt and Warma. The codiskcyclicity of $\mathfrak{A}^\mathfrak{h}_1$ results in a further density claim, related to the work of Arendt and Warma. This new approach to codiskcyclicity of operator semigroups provides a useful tool for related density claims.

The success of solar wind prediction relies heavily on accurate measurements of solar surface magnetic fields, specifically in identifying beta channels and magnetic reconnection sites. Current field measurements are limited to filling a small portion of the solar disk, but in the near future, global magnetic field maps will become available, systematically accounting for fill fraction for the entire solar surface. Despite this advancement, traditional symmetry assumptions in magnetic field mapping will no longer apply, leading to inaccurate predictions if not adapted properly. Unfortunately, traditional methods tend to introduce artificial symmetry, which can result in the misidentification of beta channels and reconnection sites. To address this issue, we've developed a new model that incorporates the effects of fill fraction on magnetic field mapping. By comparing this model to conventional methods, we found that it significantly improves the prediction of beta channels and magnetic reconnection sites, especially when the actual fill fraction is less than 50%. These results demonstrate that paying attention to fill fraction has a major impact on the mapping of solar surface magnetic fields, and that future global magnetic field maps will need to be treated carefully to achieve accurate predictions. Furthermore, we observed a close correlation between areas of significant fill fraction and the locations of beta channels and reconnection sites, as well as a clear distinction between the two in terms of fill fraction. According to our model, areas with magnetic field lines connecting the poles and beta channels have high fill fraction, while areas with reconnection sites have low fill fraction. These findings provide a foundation for refining solar wind prediction models and could also contribute to a deeper understanding of the solar corona. Additionally, this model can help explain the characteristics of solar wind streams and reconnection sites by providing a clear connection between fill fraction, magnetic topology, and plasma behavior. Ultimately, we believe that incorporating fill fraction effects into magnetic field mapping will play a crucial role in the accurate prediction of solar wind streams and reconnection sites. To achieve this, we recommend using global magnetic field maps that account for fill fraction, and also consider developing new models for predicting solar wind streams and reconnection sites based on this approach. By doing so, we may be able to accurately forecast solar wind streams and reconnection sites, even when actual data is not available, which is essential for the ongoing success of the Solar Wind Instruments Validation and Science Experiment. This experiment aims to accurately predict solar wind streams and reconnection sites from vector magnetic field maps, and provides a foundation for future experiments aimed at refining solar wind prediction models. This model and its findings have significant implications for the accurate prediction of solar wind streams and reconnection

These pairs can be used to train a language model that achieves similar performance to a model trained on labeled data, without needing massive unsupervised datasets. The ReCross method involves three primary operations: word substitution, deletion, and insertion. Our experiment shows that the methods surpasss non-contrastive unsupervised baselines and reaches par with the supervised baseline on the SuperGLUE benchmark. Additionally, the evaluation on an unsupervised dataset indicates that the model exhibits improved semantic preservation and linguistic consistency. Using data from 332,045 galaxies, we have determined the Fornax cluster's average distance to be 18.89 $\pm$ 0.07 megaparsecs (mpc) through the planetary nebulae luminosity function. This method's consistency was ensured by applying a systematic luminosity fluctuation test. The authors then used the determined distance to re-evaluate the cluster's velocity dispersion, finding it to be 539 $\pm$ 36 km/s. This velocity dispersion, coupled with the cluster's mass density, forms the mass profile that describes how mass varies with radius. The mass profile is characterized by a Navarro-Frenk White distribution with a concentration parameter of 12.89 $\pm$ 0.45. The authors then used this mass profile, combined with various stellar population models, to recompute the cluster's total mass, finding it to be 41.17 $\pm$ 2.57 billion solar masses. The authors also calculated the cluster's core radius, mass per unit core radius, and the dimensionless mass per unit core radius, and compared these results to similar findings for other local groups, demonstrating the cluster's distinct characteristics. The authors also used the cluster's mass profile to inform a simple model of its gravitational potential, using tidal radii derived from planetary nebulae in the cluster to test the model's consistency and validate its use in analyzing tidal features. The authors then used this potential to model the cluster's gravitational potential energy, considering both its stellar component and the dark matter within the cluster, and calculated the energy required to maintain its structure, finding it to be 9.53 $\pm$ 0.54 x 10^37 watts. The authors also calculated the mass accretion rate within the cluster, estimating it to be less than 0.07 solar masses per year, and used this model to predict the cluster's mass evolution over various timescales, and considered how its structure and gravitational potential may change in response to the merging of nearby galaxy clusters, such as the Virgo cluster, and the cluster's motion within the Fornax-Virgo sheet, a vast wall of galaxies that includes the Virgo cluster and spans approximately 35 megaparsecs. This paper investigates how an oblique boundary feedback with a non-zero angle affects the stability of the Navier-Stokes equations in a rectangular domain, specifically in a channel with a wedge-shaped boundary. By applying a change of coordinates, we transform the oblique feedback into a new form that includes a normal derivative term, which can be analyzed using a technique introduced by Raymond and Zarzer. With this approach, we establish that a certain inequality holds, which provides a lower bound on the growth rate of unstable modes or the decay rate of stable modes. This lower bound is determined by the cosine of the angle between the boundary and the unit vector normal to the surface, multiplied by a constant. If the angle is greater than a certain critical value, the feedback becomes stabilizing, and we can conclude that the Navier-Stokes equations have a unique stable solution on a specific time interval. This result is an extension of a previous study by Raymond and Zarzer, which considered only feedbacks with angles greater than 90 degrees. Our findings also provide a lower bound on the critical Reynolds number for turbulent flow in a wedge-shaped channel with oblique walls. Notably, when the angle approaches 180 degrees, the feedback becomes nearly isolating, and we can conclude that there is a non-trivial stable solution on an arbitrarily long time interval. Our analysis also establishes an upper bound for the first non-trivial eigenvalue of the linearized Navier-Stokes equations with oblique boundary conditions, which is of the order $\frac{1}{\cos^2 \theta}$ as the angle approaches 180 degrees. Finally, we provide a simulation of the Navier-Stokes equations with oblique boundary feedback, which confirms our theoretical findings. Our theoretical framework is then employed to investigate the topological change of the Fermi surface in Sr$_3$Ir$_2$Si$_9$ and its impact on spin susceptibility, which increases substantially with the reduction of perturbative perturbations due to intermediate and flat Fermi surface segments. Ultimately, this insight may facilitate the identification of materials exhibiting enhanced magnetic susceptibility within these levels.

In advanced driver assistance systems, a key function is providing safety-critical corrections to the driver, often utilizing a diverse range of interventions including warning sounds, visual cues, and steering corrections. These corrective actions must be tailored to accommodate various driving situations and their respective complexities. We have investigated a method to generate human-like driver guidance using natural language processing, initially applying it to two scenarios: assisting a driver merging into oncoming traffic and navigating through a pedestrian-crossing intersection. Our approach incorporated a combination of linguistic and computational techniques to create natural speech that mirrors the structure and content of human-generated text. By leveraging machine learning to analyze both spoken and written language, we were able to develop a system capable of safely correcting the driver in real-time, drawing on data from labeled audio recordings and written descriptions of driving maneuvers. In testing the system, we discovered that machine-learning trained speech sounded more appealing to human listeners than a simpler alternative but did not significantly enhance the understanding of the speech. Meanwhile, incorporating elements of both linguistic and computational approaches resulted in a more robust solution less prone to errors. Ultimately, our study demonstrated the feasibility of developing advanced driver assistance systems that utilize diverse corrective actions, aiding the driver through a multi-sensory interface. Additionally, we showed that a machine-learning trained speech generator yields a more acceptable, yet equally effective speech output when compared to a simpler alternative. Moreover, our findings highlighted the importance of integrating both natural language processing and computational techniques to create a robust speech generator capable of navigating complex driving scenarios. We also introduced a new open-source framework, called the Scene-Understanding-based Driver Guidance Framework, which is available for public use and provides a comprehensive set of tools for developing advanced driver guidance systems. This framework is an original contribution that is already showing great potential in fueling new research in this field. We have already taken the initial steps to integrate our approach with a diverse set of sensory feedback mechanisms in collaboration with industry partners. We intend to build upon these accomplishments by exploring additional techniques for creating human-like driver guidance and are seeking collaboration with like-minded researchers to advance this exciting area of research. We have made our codebase and data available at: https://github.com/alexandrv/su-driver-guidance. We look forward to contributing to this area through further research inspired by this work. We have a preliminary study published on this topic that can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.17633. By optimizing the detection order and variable gain factor, our research demonstrates that the variable gain differential detector can offer a minimum of 2.5 dB of signal-to-noise ratio improvement (SNRi) over conventional differential detection for memoryless signals and an SNRi of up to 11.5 dB for some band-limited signals with memory. Furthermore, our results show that the variable gain differential detector can provide near-optimal performance when employing two symbols of past phase information, leading to a significant 4.5 dB to 11.5 dB reduction in the required SNR compared to conventional differential detection for some band-limited signals with memory. Consequently, this implies that the variable gain differential detector can offer comparable performance to optimal coherent detection at a significantly lower signal-to-noise ratio, essentially making it a optimal coherent detection method in its own right. However, this calculation is only accurate in the thermodynamic limit and is influenced by the shape of the confining potential in finite situations. Based on the principles of correspondence, we establish a relationship between the pressure-constrained variance and a specific quantity measured in the grand canonical ensemble, namely the variance of the particle number. This relationship allows us to determine the validity of using the grand canonical ensemble by comparing the pressure-constrained variance to the size of the system. Lastly, we outline the scope for extending these results to more complex systems. In this study, we examine the model companionship phenomenon within set theory, depending on the signature in which set theory is formulated. Our analysis reveals that when set theory is defined using a specific signature, consisting of symbols for equality and membership, it exhibits model companionship within a particular class of structures that can be characterized as arbitrary transitive models of a certain set-theoretic axiom system. However, when the signature is expanded to include additional constants, this model companionship property is lost. Moreover, for each individual constant added to the signature, we can find a distinct universe that is a model of the extended set theory but does not share a strong similarity with any model of the original set theory. These distinct universes also exhibit a different strong similarity with models of a modified set theory, where the original set theory has been extended by a different constant each time. Finally, we discuss how the relationship between these universes can be seen as an example of strong similarity across different first-order theories, when those theories are viewed as defined through their interpretation within the language of predicate logic. This research is ultimately geared towards exploring the potential applications to the study of relations between different universes or models of various first-order theories. It also paves the way for a more comprehensive investigation into the model companionship phenomenon within set theory, when defined within various signatures, particularly one that includes just the standard set-theoretic language, comprised of symbols for equality and membership. This latter investigation is presented in a companion paper. That companion paper also reports on the effective implementation of a decision procedure for the model companionship problem within the context of this latter system, where the query whether a given sentence is consistent with a specific model companionship of ZFC has a response, as does whether it is a theorem of the model companionship of ZFC, via an algorithm that draws upon the Bachi-Bueckenvald decision procedure for the syllogistic fragment of first-order logic with identity, when expressed in a specific signature. This effective decision procedure for the model companionship problem of ZFC is made possible by an appropriate formulation of the Tarski sequence for each specific model, in addition to an appropriate formulation of the Lowenheim-Skolem theorem, when the scope of the quantifiers is the entire universe, along with the application of a relevant theorem from the theory of arithmetical functions. We analyzed 18 years of data on psychoactive prescription prescriptions in a large regional healthcare system from 2000 to 2018. Our data set consists of prescriptions filled by over 1.2 million individuals, containing information on the amount of 18 different substances prescribed, such as opioid analgesics, benzodiazepines, and sedatives, that are commonly abused. It is essential to measure the consumption of individual substances in relation to all others, which we calculate using a method that corrects for both prescription quantities and user counts. By applying this approach, we found that the consumption of some drugs correlated strongly with the consumption of other drugs. Specifically, prescription patterns for different classes of drugs, such as heroin and synthetic opioids, or benzodiazepines and sedatives, showed significant correlation levels (p<0.001), according to pairwise correlations computed over monthly time frames. Nevertheless, our analysis revealed that the consumption of these substances does not follow a coordinated pattern. Instead, the development of an individual substance's consumption is independent, as demonstrated by the lack of significant autocorrelation (p>0.05) within the same class for all substances examined, with the exception of the synthetic opioids, which showed a minor trend of increased correlation in later years. These findings may provide valuable insights into the complexities of the drug abuse problem and could benefit from further exploration within the context of theoretical models that explain the development of drug consumption. As a broader perspective, our method for measuring the consumption of controlled substances could be applied to any data set containing prescription information and thus has implications for research into the epidemiology of drug abuse. However, using attention in automated speech recognition systems to capture the relationships between speech representations and linguistic context has been shown to be less efficient. This is because speech representations and linguistic context are often processed in tandem during decoding, limiting the effectiveness of attention in these situations. This study introduces the bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM), a novel attention mechanism that allows the transfer of learning from linguistic context to speech representations and vice versa. BiAM was incorporated into a non-recurrent, encoder-decoder framework and assessed in zero-shot learning scenarios. The results showed that BiAM successfully leverages linguistic context to enhance the exchange of information between speech representations and context, resulting in superior performance compared to baseline attention mechanisms. Compared to conventional attention, BiAM led to significant reductions in error rates of zero-shot learning, with reductions of 13.3% and 11.6% on Fisher and COQA datasets respectively. The plasmon behavior at closer twists is more sensitive to lattice structure, particularly in regions where doping effects dominate. Deep neural language models have revolutionized the field of natural language processing, achieving exceptional performance in various tasks and capturing intricate language nuances. Despite their success, there remains a gap in understanding how these models perceive the hierarchical structure of sentences. Sequential models operate by analyzing nearby words in a sentence and relying on local heuristics to identify contextual relationships. As such, it's plausible they can capture the syntactic dependencies evident in sentence structure. In this research, we investigate the ability of deep neural language models to recognize the hierarchical structure of sentences through sequential reduction, where we sequentially remove words from the beginning or end of a sentence and observe how the models' predictions change. Our results show that models pre-trained on contextual tasks are highly sensitive to the sequential reduction of words in a sentence and can distinguish between local and global heuristics. Moreover, our findings indicate that the sensitivity of these models to sequential reduction is correlated with their sensitivity to local and global heuristics. To further explore this phenomenon, we develop a cognitive task that assesses the ability of these models to recognize the hierarchical structure of sentences. Our results from both automated evaluations and human assessments confirm that high-sensitivity models better mimic human performance on this task. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that sequential reduction offers an effective methodology for investigating the ability of deep neural language models to recognize the hierarchical structure of sentences. By utilizing this methodology, we are able to design better pre-training objectives that enhance the sensitivity of these models to local and global heuristics. In doing so, we are one step closer to developing a theoretical framework that explains how deep neural language models capture the syntactic dependencies evident in sentence structure. This framework has far-reaching implications, enabling us to decompose the complexity of sentence structure into a sequence of local and global heuristics. To facilitate future research, we introduce the Languid toolkit, a comprehensive software package that includes all sequential reduction tasks, cognitive evaluations, and the models and objectives explored in this research. This toolkit is available for download at https://github.com/ghulame/languid. All sequential reduction tasks and cognitive evaluations have been approved for a low-risk classification according to the University at Buffalo's Institutional Review Board standards.
