To tackle this challenge, we present a groundbreaking series of experiments designed to provide valuable insights into players' behaviors when engaging with gamified physical therapy exercises. By analyzing users' real-world interactions with our previously developed physical therapy gamified systems, we conducted a comprehensive empirical study to gain a deeper understanding of how interactions are perceived in relation to their functional aspects. This theoretical framework, informed by our findings, introduces a new multidimensional concept called Perception-Function Balance (PFB), which serves as a cohesive framework for categorizing the perceptions of rehabilitation interactions. By applying the PFB model to our empirical data, we identified several prominent factors that influence PFB, including clarity, clarity of goals, challenge levels, feedback, and sedentary versus active elements, which can aid developers in creating rehabilitation games that achieve a perfect balance between engaging players and meeting their therapeutic objectives. Furthermore, our research provides a foundation for conducting similar empirical studies on various rehabilitation games, which can contribute to a broader understanding of how to design interactive elements for these types of games. By joining our existing methodology for categorizing rehabilitation games into four categories based on their goals, the PFB model now offers a comprehensive framework for classifying the perceptions of rehabilitation games within these categories. Ultimately, our research can serve as a starting point for conducting more in-depth analyses of the preferences of different patient populations in relation to various rehabilitation exercises and games. By joining our existing research on the functional aspects of rehabilitation interactions, our findings can contribute to a unified theoretical framework for classifying both the perceptions and functional aspects of rehabilitation games. This, in turn, can facilitate the development of a taxonomy for the numerous types of active and sedentary elements found in rehabilitation games. By doing so, this taxonomy can provide a set of best-practice guidelines for creating engaging and effective rehabilitation games that consider both the clinical objectives of these games and the preferences of their players. Consequently, this research has the potential to shape the future design of rehabilitation games, thus contributing to a broader understanding of how to create interactive elements for these games. Our research investigates the theoretical underpinnings of a nonlinear elasticity model that incorporates both geometric nonlinearity and linearised elasticity within a brittle fracture framework. To achieve this, we draw upon the concept of two-phase materials, where both phases represent distinct elasticity regimes. A specific vector field is introduced to differentiate between linearised elasticity and geometric nonlinearity, and relevant energy functionals are formulated accordingly. Furthermore, we establish the minimal regularity properties of maps that minimize specific nonlinear elasticity models, where this analysis involves linearised elasticity within a geometric nonlinearity framework. Specifically, we demonstrate that in a geometric nonlinearity framework, maps with minimal energy under linearised elasticity constraints possess a specific degree of differentiability, whereas this higher degree of differentiability is lost when considering geometric nonlinearity. A key component of our argument involves an equilibrium problem that arises from extracting bounds, as well as an analysis of the stability of these equilibrium problems across different elasticity regimes. Notably, our results provide a mathematical foundation for recent numerical approximations of nonlinear elasticity models within a geometric nonlinearity framework. Our research also offers an explicit solution to a specific extraction problem, where this solution involves a unique equilibrium state that can be characterized through a specific volume-form expression. Moreover, our findings imply that multiple-line fracture patterns can be obtained as optimal minimizers for specific nonlinear elasticity models that incorporate both geometric nonlinearity and linearised elasticity under certain boundary conditions. Lastly, our analysis includes a discussion on the role of linearised elasticity as a linearised limit-case of geometric nonlinearity, where this discussion involves an explicit description of the associated transition layer when considering maps that minimise specific energy functionals. Our research thus offers a comprehensive exploration of nonlinear elasticity models within a geometric nonlinearity framework, where this study provides an explicit analysis of both model components - geometric nonlinearity and linearised elasticity - as well as a discussion on their interplay. Consequently, our findings can be viewed as a classification theorem for nonlinear elasticity models within a geometric nonlinearity framework, where this classification is based upon the coexistence of both geometric nonlinearity and linearised elasticity across distinct energy scales. Consequently, our research offers a theoretical underpinning for further numerical approximation schemes of nonlinear elasticity models within a geometric nonlinearity framework. Our research is particularly relevant to the 'linearisation by layer' hypothesis that has emerged from recent numerical approximations of nonlinear elasticity models, where this hypothesis proposes that linearised elasticity is equivalent to a specific transition layer problem for maps that minimise specific energy functionals.

Accurate location tracking within complex indoor areas relies heavily on WiFi fingerprinting techniques. While these methods are effective, they are prone to geographical distance estimations with substantial errors. By leveraging supervised machine learning models, we can utilize existing WiFi fingerprint databases to enhance the precision of geospatial location predictions. We focus on a filling pattern where electron bunches from various passes share the same training threshold, and consider an application where an intermediate RF cavity influences the threshold current.
Our analysis shows that the choice of filling pattern affects beam-RF interaction and threshold current in a significant way.
Furthermore, we find that the location of an intermediate RF cavity can optimize recovery efficiency by balancing the impact on threshold current and the energy captured.

Our previous research suggested that a temperature range of approximately 10-50 K is likely optimal for the formation of planetesimals, as it allows for a significant increase in sticking forces in extremely dry samples, which can sustain up to ten times more tension before breaking. This finding has implications for models of planetesimal formation, which often rely on particles sticking together in low-temperature environments. However, these models typically ignore variations in composition and instead focus on two-dimensional simulations, which do not account for differences in sticking and fragmentation in three-dimensional scenarios. In this follow-up study, we use three-dimensional simulations to explore how variations in sticking and fragmentation affect the growth of planetesimals in dry and wet conditions. Our models show that in dry environments, high tensions enable particles to stick together efficiently, leading to a rapid growth of planetesimals through gravitational accumulation. In contrast, wet conditions result in fragmented particles that cannot stick together effectively, leading to a slower growth of planetesimals through collisional accretion. These outcomes align with previous predictions made by other researchers and further support the idea that a distinction should be drawn between collisional accretion in wet conditions and gravitational accumulation in dry environments. Our models also highlight the importance of distinguishing between primary and secondary planetesimals, as well as the need to differentiate between dry and wet environments in models of the solar system. Finally, our research suggests that the solar system's primary planetesimals formed through gravitational accumulation in a dry environment, while secondary planetesimals, such as those in our own solar system, may have formed through collisional accretion in a wet environment. This could have significant implications for our understanding of the solar system's final stages of formation. Lastly, we propose that future experiments should focus on further exploring the sticking and fragmentation of solid particles in various compositions and temperatures, as well as investigating how these processes are influenced by other factors such as magnetic fields and gas phases. These experiments could provide valuable insights into how to optimize planetesimal formation through gravitational accumulation in dry environments, as well as shed light on the long-standing question of when and how heavy grains can stick together effectively in various astrophysical contexts. Robot skills are often governed by rules that must be followed to maintain safety and effectiveness. Unfortunately, traditional imitation learning methods fail to account for these complex nonlinear restrictions due to their linearized treatment. A novel paradigm, constrained imitation learning, has been developed to tackle this issue by directly addressing hard constraints. However, existing conformance measures are limited to linear boundaries or quadratic penalties, hindering their application to complex robot tasks. To overcome this limitation, a new approach is proposed that allows for nonlinear boundary constraints represented through smooth function fields. A demonstration showcases the performance of this method on a complex robot task involving the constraining of nonlinear boundaries in a high-dimensional space. Results from various trials indicate that the proposed technique achieves a level of precision that is comparable to that of constraint-free imitation learning transfers. Furthermore, the ability of this method to accommodate diverse constraint specifications is also highlighted through the incorporation of an intuitive graphical user interface. The code has been made publicly accessible for further exploration and extension. Through the integration of this approach, a wide range of complex robot tasks governed by various nonlinear constraints can be efficiently automated through imitation learning. The proposed technique also provides a foundation for the investigation of new conformance measures that can inform the design of future robot learning algorithms. Using an expansion of super Yang-Mills theory in $\mathcal{N}=4$, we derive a contact term equation for two gluon contact operators, confirmed by an algebraic method, and find that a specific two gluon contact operator shares the same colour component with one component of six gluon amplitude contact operators in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. We also establish an relationship between the two gluon contact operators and the six gluon amplitude contact operators by integrating the former into the latter, and demonstrate that the two gluon contact operators are singular enough to generate the six gluon amplitude contact operators through a colour organised procedure. We further demonstrate that the two gluon contact operators can be represented by a colour organised, singular part of a bosonisation operator which produces a six gluon amplitude from an arbitrary super Yang-Mills field, and discuss implications for amplitude growth in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. We conclude by considering the two gluon contact operators in a general $\mathcal{N}=K$ super Yang-Mills theory. We assess the topological features of Sr$_2$MgGe$_2$ by combining spin-orbit coupling and superconductivity, using a 3D tight-binding model and wavelength-independent perturbation theory to analyze the disorder effects. The quantitative topological inferences are made by comparing the ratios of disorder-induced shifts in superconducting state energies to those of a topological state energy at zero energy. Our findings indicate that the spin-orbit coupling plays a significant role in realizing the strong-topological-insulator phase, whereas the superconductivity alone cannot be responsible for this phase due to the absence of pair-spin rotation symmetry, and that the interaction between spin-orbit coupling and superconductivity leads to a non-trivial topological state with non-zero texture of the order parameter. Moreover, we observe that the non-trivial topological state is separated from the trivial state by a threshold of spin-orbit coupling of approximately 10.4 millieV, and that the ratio of disorder-induced shifts exhibits a distinct variation with respect to the spin-orbit coupling. Finally, we propose that Sr$_2$MgGe$_2$ is an ideal candidate material to experimentally investigate strong-topological superconductivity via hole-doping.

By integrating a highly anisotropic $d$-wave interaction at the Fermi surface, our theory reveals a distinct rotation of the vortex lattice angles $\theta$ and $\phi$ in response to pressure. Near the critical point of the van Hove singularity, the vortex lattice behavior exhibits an unexpected abrupt change at the predicted critical pressure $p_{\rm crit}$, distinguishing it from the proposed $T^2$-pressure relationship. Instead, our model indicates that the vortex lattice transition is directly linked to $p_{\rm crit}$ through a pair of distinct angles $\theta_0$ and $\phi_0$, which emerge only when the van Hove singularity is taken into consideration. The proposed theory is supported by two distinct approaches to calculating the vortex lattice angles: first through the direct minimization of the free energy in the London gauge, and second through the application of a Ginzburg-Landau type expansion near the critical point. Given a finite connected graph G and an integer k, the k-truncated geodesic distance is defined as the set of all pairs of nodes in G with a distance of k or less. We denote this as G^k. A recent study proposed using truncated geodesic distance to determine the structure of a graph. In this work, we investigate the metric dimension of graphs that have been truncated at a certain distance threshold. We first establish that for any connected finite graph G and any integer k, the metric dimension of G^k is equal to the maximum metric dimension of G's connected components. This implies that to study G^k, it is sufficient to focus on the subgraphs induced by nodes that can be reached from a particular starting node in k steps. We then investigate the metric dimension of various graph types that have been truncated at specific distance thresholds. We discuss the tractability of computing the metric dimension of truncated graphs and explore some general properties of G^k. We also investigate the relationship between G^k and G's subgraphs, particularly those with the largest girth k. Notably, we prove that when k is 1 or 2, the graph G^k is perfect, meaning its clique number is equal to its chromatic number. We also find that for graphs that have been truncated at a distance of 3 or more, there is no similar perfect graph theorem. We provide examples of graphs whose truncated versions G^k have a perfect clique structure, but G^k itself is not perfect. We also explore the relationship between G^k and G's cut number. The Gondwana supercontinent began to break apart around 180 million years ago during the Jurassic period, resulting in the separation of Africa, South America, Australia, India, and Antarctica from around 180 to 80 million years ago. This process involved several episodes of rift activity, with significant extensions occurring along the Tanama Basin on South America and the Karoo Basin on Africa. These areas experienced a unique type of marginal architecture, characterized by a bended pattern of sedimentary basins and volcanic provinces. Initially, a direct rift-related geometry was present, but it transformed into a more complex configuration due to changes in extension direction and velocity, leading to the formation of lateral links, constraints, and faults that played a crucial role in the placement of volcanic provinces. This paper explores the influence of changes in extension direction and velocity on the development of these marginal structures through the Karoo and Tanama basins, combining analytical and numerical techniques to model their behavior. Ultimately, this work offers a novel approach to analyzing complex marginal architecture, which can be applied to various areas around the world. Language evolves continually, with new words emerging, old meanings fading, and a middle ground of innovative semantic transformations.  Despite its ubiquity, this evolution goes largely unnoticed, as the processes that drive it are complex and hard to quantify.  This study leverages vast language models to uncover previously unknown neologisms and semantic shifts.  By finetuning models on graded semantic evaluations from thousands of users, we reveal numerous examples of emerging words, declining word meanings, and semantic extensions.  We also establish practical criteria for identifying words with significant meaning change and validate these criteria across multiple datasets.  Our discovery toolkit comprises simple, model-agnostic methods that can be applied to any word or phrase for which we have a clear definition.  By harnessing vast datasets of licensed text, we find many novel word meanings and shifts confirmed through offline dictionaries and lexical repositories.  Our work lays the foundation for an ongoing research project, with the code and data available at https://github.com/hahnfridrik/finding-change, where we outline steps for contributing new findings.  As the project evolves, we plan to integrate additional resources and knowledge.  In the short term, we hope to expand our discovery toolkit by incorporating additional methods and validating our criteria across more datasets.  With these tools, we aim to facilitate public participation in documenting language change.  We invite you to explore our work and contribute your own discoveries to help build a comprehensive repository of ongoing language evolution.  You can do so by visiting our website at https://change.fridrik.hahn.is/.  We look forward to collaborating with you in uncovering the continuous changes shaping our languages.  By working together, we can create a rich, dynamic, and freely accessible archive of new words, shifting meanings, and innovative semantic transformations.  This joint effort will provide invaluable insights into the complex processes driving language evolution and serve as a valuable resource for both words and phrases.  As such, it has the potential to greatly benefit both lexical theory and the development of cutting-edge natural language processing models. Recent studies in generating counterfactual data have focused on crafting scenarios that could have occurred, yet such methods often produce divergent results when applied to more complex settings. A novel algorithm called DISCO is introduced, enabling the creation of counterfactual data that generalizes to greater variability, especially when applied to machine learning models. By utilizing a counterfactual generation framework that incorporates both a primary model and a contrast function, DISCO crafts scenarios that, while remaining physically plausible, significantly raise doubts about the original classification. Multiple experiments demonstrate that training with counterfactual data generated by DISCO enhances both robustness and generalization when applied to complex settings, such as image classification and graph classification. The results show that while existing methods lead to model drift and decreases generalization, in contrast, DISCO preserves generalization and boosts robustness. Additionally, we find that these counterfactual scenarios are not only morally contentious but also empirically prone to causing the model to fail. A robustness generalization metric is also introduced to better evaluate these aspects. Overall, our findings highlight the advantages of employing counterfactual data generated by DISCO in machine learning, leading to more reliable models with increased variability. A theoretical analysis is also provided, showcasing that these generated counterfactuals can be viewed as perturbing the original input in a direction that is both physically plausible and morally contentious. A practical application of this is a demonstration that these counterfactuals can be used to create morally contentious attacks on machine learning models in real-world scenarios. A implementation of our algorithm is available online.

Main idea: Multi-label product categorization involves assigning a product to more than one category, but this makes data annotation extremely difficult because the number of possible combinations explodes with each new category added.

To tackle this challenge, the idea is to train a model that can learn from single-label and multi-label data simultaneously by introducing a novel data sampling method called S2M.

This method allows a single label to act as a primary label and all other relevant labels as secondary labels, effectively turning single-label data into multi-label data.

By doing so, the model can benefit from both the abundance of single-label data and the rare multi-label data by minimizing the explosion of possible combinations.

Experiments on real-world datasets show that this approach outperforms current state-of-the-art models using existing data sampling methods.

In particular, the model performs especially well when there's a large gap between single-label and multi-label annotations. 

The S2M method also allows the model to effectively utilize hard multi-label samples, i.e. those with a balance of positive and negative labels, resulting in a significant improvement in accuracy. 

The proposed approach is versatile and compatible with various deep learning architectures, such as deep neural networks and convolutional neural networks. 

Finally, an analysis of the sampling process provides valuable insights into the optimal data distribution for multi-label product categorization. 

This work is the first to introduce a multi-label product categorization dataset called Tmall, which comprises over 1 million product descriptions and their corresponding multi-label annotations.

In recruitment, interviews and panels are frequently arranged with a limited number of candidates per position, which often results in similar tasks needing to be performed by the same individuals. Due to the comprehensive assessment provided by the panel interview, selecting the most suitable panel members is particularly crucial. In this context, we have developed an algorithm that expedites the panel selection process, allowing recruiters to promptly obtain the most suitable panel candidates based on prior evaluations, which can be done in real-time. Furthermore, we have designed a method to promptly generate alternative panel lists in accordance with existing guidelines. We have implemented both methods using a parametric optimization technique and a sorting algorithm, which demonstrate excellent performance, requiring only a few seconds to compute even for relatively large datasets. We have evaluated our proposed methods through real-world scenarios and findings, presenting them in the form of a tool accessible via this link https://panelrecruit.surge.sh/. Additionally, we demonstrated that our model's performance in predicting future expression states is on par with that of simpler, static models. Nutating Galaxy-NUclei (NUGgets) are an uncommon category of extreme starburst galaxies characterized by a rotating galaxy nucleus with two bright, nucleated arms. I study one such NUGget, a highly inclined, moderate-redshift galaxy, using high-resolution spectroscopy and far-infrared imagery. Observations indicate a massive, face-on disk of atomic and molecular gas rotating at the same speed as 1.4 GHz radio emission, but with prominent outflows in both gas phases along the galaxy's minor axis. A circumgalactic medium analysis reveals gas reservoirs in the host galaxy's surrounding area, which are characterized by low density and slow rotation. Certain CI line emissions serve as indicators of gas reservoirs or outflows, distinguishing between the two based on velocity and line shape. Findings suggest that massive starbursts with rotating nucleus planes may be associated with circumgalactic gas reservoirs, indicating that such reservoirs are formed through the rejection of gas due to the rotating galaxy's gravitational forces. Our findings demonstrate that HPN achieves higher accuracy across multiple datasets in both single-instrument and multi-instrument classification tasks, outperforming the baseline prototypical network. Furthermore, our experiment showcasing the interpretation of hierarchical prototypes reveals that HPN derives benefit from the hierarchical loss function in the form of increased accuracy in interim category classification, along with a correlation between the most prominent prototype of an interim category and the average feature of the corresponding instruments belonging to that category. This suggests that HPN is capable of identifying distinct prototypes for distinct categories and subcategories. Additionally, our model exhibits a preference for aggregating prototype features from higher-level categories rather than lower-level categories in the hierarchical setting. Moreover, our experiment indicates that the hierarchical organization of prototypes, coupled with hierarchical loss calculation and feature aggregation, results in enhanced classification performance, along with decreased reliance on prototype features from lower-level categories. Acronyms pose a challenge for both humans and artificial intelligence due to their condensed and often ambiguous nature. While many acronyms can be easily deciphered, others require additional context from the surrounding sentence or section, and some are even explicitly defined in documents. Current methods typically rely on context but often fail when acronyms are novel or their reference is unclear. Furthermore, most existing approaches focus solely on decoding single acronyms, neglecting situations where multiple acronyms are intertwined and need to be disambiguated simultaneously. To address these limitations, we propose building a system that leverages domain-specific knowledge to both identify and disambiguate acronyms in various writing styles. Our proposed system consists of two primary components: one that exploits domain knowledge to classify acronyms and their references, and another that employs a disambiguation network to decode acronyms in context. To train and evaluate our system, we create a large dataset consisting of 19,000 documents with annotated acronyms in three categories (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics domains, news domain, and general domain). Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed system achieves superior performance on unknown acronyms when compared to existing methods but fails to generalize well to domains different from the training data. This could facilitate the development of a universal primer format for DNA data storage. Our algorithm is available as a resource for the community to utilize and further develop. Our research discovers a novel class of nodal lines in the momentum space, found in a 2D lattice constructed from slightly distorted herringbone patterns, and characterized by continuous curves passing through both high-symmetry points and irregular areas. This distinct feature sets nodal lines apart from other topological states, which are confined to high-symmetry locations. By carefully modifying the lattice structure, we gradually close the nodal lines, transforming them into isolated points within the Brillouin zone. A comprehensive review of deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) and their variations applied to deinterlacing is provided in this paper. Most existing work focused on real-time deinterlacing, leveraging advanced algorithms, often surpassing traditional methods. To enhance deinterlacing efficiency, our research proposed a simple, lightweight network (SLN) utilizing an extensive training dataset. The proposed SLN consisted of three key components: an initial downsampling layer, three repetitive residual blocks, and an upscaling layer. To mitigate overfitting, a technique involving random axis-aligned rotation and cropping was employed. Moreover, we developed a real-time SLN (RLN) by reducing the number of parameters and incorporating a training method involving data fine-tuning. Comparative evaluations revealed that both the proposed SLN and RLN outperformed current real-time deinterlacing frameworks in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM). Additionally, the SLN and RLN demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional methods, particularly in low-resolution environments. Notably, the RLN achieved comparable performance to the SLN while utilizing significantly fewer parameters. As a result, the proposed SLN and RLN are highly suitable for various video deinterlacing applications. The source codes of the proposed SLN and RLN are available online at https://github.com/hihiroki/Deinterlacing-SLN-RLN.

The increasing miniaturization of acoustic technologies necessitates a microscopic-scale understanding of thermoviscous effects, which involve the interaction of acoustic flow and boundary layer properties in liquids. This knowledge is crucial for designing acoustic metamaterials and manipulating energy at the microscopic scale. Research has progressed in visualizing thermoviscous effects, particularly in the acoustic boundary layer, through direct simulation of the Navier-Stokes equations. This study employs a novel numerical framework to investigate the acoustic boundary layer's impact on energy transport in a microscopic acoustic metamaterial. The investigation focuses on a two-dimensional microchannel with alternating acoustic resonance cavities, controlled by a thin diaphragm. This setup creates a lateral pressure gradient influencing energy transport and extinction of acoustic multiples. The findings show that thermoviscous effects intensify energy transport in the boundary layer by increasing the Reynolds contribution, whereas flow confinement contributes less than anticipated. Additionally, this study reveals how acoustic meta-materials' energy transport properties can be modulated through flow confinement, resonance in the microchannel, and acoustic driving pressure. This work lays the groundwork for further exploration of thermoviscous effects in acoustic meta-materials and provides a numerical framework for investigating other complicated micro acoustic systems. This study's findings also highlight the significance of considering both acoustic and viscous interactions when designing microscopic acoustic technologies. To address this, we develop a method to derive non-Gaussian distributions for joint fluctuations in concentration and a related quantity, where one is directly linked to the diffusion coefficients of the other. This is achievable through the use of joint joint diffusion equations that we obtain from a detailed analysis of diffusion coefficient fluctuations. Our approach enables the evaluation of non-Gaussian effects in various ways, including through the behavior of the second cumulant, which we then apply to specific scenarios like the diffusion of charged particles in Stokes flows and the diffusion of mixtures of solvents and solutes. By considering the effects of gradients, correlations, and variations on the second cumulant, we provide a unified framework for assessing the validity of Gaussian approximations in these situations. Unlike previous GAN models, this approach utilizes a combination of spatial and spectral features extracted by convolutional and Fourier neural operators to create realistic synthetic turbulent signals. To train and evaluate the model, we utilize data from direct numerical simulation of turbulent flow in a channel at various high Reynolds numbers, specifically $1875$, $3750$, and $7500$. The results show that the model excels at mimicking turbulent signals across all observed Reynolds numbers, even when tested with data from an unseen category. Notably, the output of the model demonstrates similar performance to that of physics-based models when compared to direct observations of turbulent velocity profiles. However, there are some differences evident at the smallest scales, likely due to the limited resolution of the model. The findings also indicate that increasing the resolution of the model does not significantly improve its performance, and introducing an extra convolutional layer leads to diminished performance. The introduction of an additional spectral feature extractor in the generator leads to diminished performance, and the model excels at generating realistic turbulent signals even without incorporating spectral information. This scenario, which includes spontaneous emission and interactions with the atoms, is numerically solved to determine eigenstates and eigenenergies of the system. We show that, for an excited state of a single atom, the emission rate displays an $n^3$ dependence on the position within the series, highlighting the complex interplay between collective phenomena and atomic properties in this context. This study provides a theoretical basis for understanding the electronic environment of atoms interacting with a multimode laser field. It also paves the way for a new perspective on the Ritz variation method when applied to this type of system. Traditional deep neural network classifiers, despite achieving high accuracy rates, are prone to a significant drawback: they can't accurately predict their own confidence levels when confronted with uncertain or manipulable input. This deficiency stems from the training process, where the model is typically optimized to minimize a loss function while being forced to adhere to a hard label constraint. In contrast, our study proposes a distinct objective function based on scaling, which treats the predicted probability distribution as a continuous means of assessing model performance. By leveraging the capabilities of optimal transport theory, we can determine the extent to which two probability distributions diverge, which provides a coherent way to measure uncertainty or prediction error. This new approach, which we refer to as the generalized expected Hamiltonian distance (GEHD), facilitates learning robust and trustworthy models through regularization-based methods while enabling true-out-of-distribution (TOD) detection by defining a boundary based on average prediction error. Our experimental results demonstrate notable improvements in TOD detection and robust performance on various datasets, solidifying the GEHD's potential as a unifying framework for enhancing the reliability of deep neural networks. Furthermore, our study incorporates theoretical insights into the issues of model precision and data sampling. The code for our research is openly accessible on the GitHub platform.

Our findings highlight the inconsistencies that can arise from traditional evaluation methods and suggest that the best performers tend to be robust in our evolving environment. We investigate a one-dimensional quasiperiodic system based on the Fibonacci sequence, which exhibits a reentrant transition between light localization and delocalization. Our analysis, which considers an infinite number of nearest neighbors for the propagation of light, reveals that this complex behavior can be qualitatively understood through a simple principle: when a certain threshold of coupling between nearby sites is exceeded, there is a sudden shift from localized to delocalized states. This finding is supported by two methods of calculation: by directly solving the equations that describe the behavior of light in the Fibonacci system and by using an analytical approach that breaks down the localization transition into smaller, coupled units of increasing complexity. Our study provides a theoretical basis for a broader applicability of this reentrant behavior in two-dimensional Parise-MacKay lattices to any self-similar localization pattern found in one-dimensional quasiperiodic systems. Using observations from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the SDSS-IV, we examine the relationship between the near-ultraviolet color of 460,000+ galaxies and their mass under conditions similar to those of the GALEV model. For galaxies below a mass threshold of approximately $\log (M_{\rm gal}/M_\odot) = 10.6$, the NUV-r color becomes more negative as galaxy mass increases, a trend that holds across various stellar combinations and environmental settings simulated by GALEV. However, above this mass threshold, NUV-r color ceases to exhibit a clear correlation with mass and instead follows a color of approximately 0.92 \pm 0.06, regardless of mass. We examine a restricted version of the Erdős-Turán conjecture, which concerns subsets of integers containing few members of an arithmetic progression. Unlike the original conjecture, this version allows a finite number (denoted as 'h') of summands in its definition, and we aim to determine the minimum value ('f(h)') that guarantees the subset's density within the integers is non-negligible, where 'h' serves as the maximum size of an arithmetic progression. Our research establishes a lower bound for 'f(h)' of at least $h^2$ and suspects that this lower bound could be as low as 'h'. To validate this hypothesis, we need to show that there exists a highly dense subset of integers exhibiting the 'h'-AP property and a substantial gap between 'f(3)' and 'f(4)'. This achievement not only fills a prominent gap in the Erdős-Turán conjecture but also resolves a significant subproblem of Gowers's problem about distinct arithmetic progressions. Additionally, our results demonstrate that the density 'f(h)' can be achieved through a construction based on an irreducible polynomial of a specific form over a finite field and further imply that the density of a three-term AP within the integers is greater than $16$. Furthermore, we found an upper limit for $\pi(x)$ that exhibits quads and it is higher than $\pi(x)/16$. This development represents a crucial step towards a more comprehensive theory of sets defined by multiple arithmetic progressions and offers a framework that can be applied to various mathematical problems involving minimal systems of equations in polynomials over a finite field. This framework can also be utilized to address questions related to the density of systems of equations in polynomials over a finite field and may have implications for problems involving square-free numbers, highly composite numbers, and their equivalents within a finite field. Lastly, our research introduces a new concept, the 'density function of systems of equations', which can be applied to any system of equations defined by algebraic expressions and enables the study of such systems within the context of number theory. This work is accompanied by a groundbreaking lower limit for the density of four-term APs ($f(4) \geq 42589$) that has an extraordinary magnitude compared to the density of three-term APs ($f(3) = 9$). This significant difference in densities highlights an extensive gap between two instances of the Erdős-Turán conjecture and this achievement was achieved by constructing a highly dense subset of integers

Using the WKB method, we perform an analysis of classical chaotic behavior for the Hénon-Heiles model with a perturbing force from the harmonic oscillator, focusing on a region where this behavior transitions from orderly to chaotic. Our calculations provide ground-state energy estimates and probability density patterns within the associated classical resonances, revealing how these patterns change in response to increasing perturbation strength and how they mirror the dynamics observed in purely classical simulations. Furthermore, our results show that classical melting orbits can be accounted for through nonadiabatic effects in the classical motion, revealing that classical hyperbolic trajectories can survive somewhat intact in this context. In addition, our analysis includes a comparison of our approach to other semiclassical methods, such as the monodromy matrix technique, and highlights the similarities and differences that arise when applying these methods to this particular problem. Lastly, we discuss potential applications of this understanding to the study of other complex quantum systems.

enhance healthcare resource allocation. To support this goal, we propose an
approach to predicting ICU demand based on data from incoming patients.
Specifically, we recommend identifying key features related to ICU admission
and prostate cancer treatment features, and using decision trees to estimate
the likelihood of a patient needing ICU care. To evaluate this approach, we
use data from the MIMIC-III dataset and MCCI dataset, covering aspects of
COVID-19 patient care. Our results show a strong correlation between predicted
and actual ICU stays, and demonstrate the effectiveness of featuring cancer
treatment in the model. To further enhance this approach, we suggest
incorporating temporal data and enhancing machine learning algorithms.
Additionally, we highlight potential applications and highlight areas for
future research in this field. The code for this project is available on
GitHub under the name ICU-Prediction.

We compared the performance of three types of models, namely Tensors, Graphs, and a combination of both, for supervised action recognition tasks. Our experiments demonstrated that combined models are capable of achieving competitive results with minimal representation on graph structures. Specifically, when applying a simple graph representation, using both tensor and graph representations yielded a 2% reduction in error rate compared to using tensor representation alone. Additionally, this finding was robust across various training dataset sizes, movement speed rates, and movement complexity levels. We observed a notable increase in performance with larger training datasets, suggesting that the benefits of combined models are more pronounced in real-world applications. Our work provides a preliminary exploration of this concept, laying the groundwork for future research in motion understanding. We have made our code and data available for public use at https://github.com/strmln/Action-Recognition-with-Tensors-and-Graphs. Our work has been presented at the 31st British Machine Vision Conference (BMVC 2020).

This paper describes a high-performance, parallel search engine known as the Content Addressable Parallel Processor (CPP). The CPP is capable of locating complete strings or partial string patterns within a stored database of 512 bytes. It establishes communication with a host computer through a parallel interface and can be programmed using the C++ programming language via the GNU C++ compiler. By utilizing the <cpp.h> header file, which includes parallel interface functions, the CPP can be programmed efficiently. The provided software includes the CPP driver, software that allows for communication between the CPP and the host computer, and is compatible with Linux operating systems. The included example programs demonstrate how to utilize the CPP driver for various CPP operations. The CPP's performance is evaluated by conducting several test searches under different scenarios and its results are presented. The evaluation shows that the CPP's speed is substantially faster than the host computer when searching for strings within the stored database. However, the CPP's speed may be comparable to that of the host computer when searching for patterns in smaller datasets. The software mentioned in this paper can be obtained through the address http://sourceforge.net/projects/cpp/. The CPP's performance is comparable to other content addressable parallel computers discussed in the literature. Our analysis focuses on the effects of accretion on galaxy structure and stellar composition using a suite of high-resolution, gas-rich, major merger simulations. These simulations, incorporating advanced submodels for gas dynamics and star formation, allow for a detailed exploration of merger phases and remnants. Our theoretical framework is validated against similar models and established through comparative analysis of our results with prior studies. Our findings show that the accumulation of gas during a merger leads to enhanced stellar formation and an increase in stellar mass for both participating galaxies. However, the central cores of these galaxies experience rapid gas depletion due to gravitational interactions, limiting further stellar generation. Our data reveal a diverse range of galaxy architectures resulting from the structural reorganization induced by the merger. This includes the formation of bulges and the disruption of existing ones, along with the generation of ring-like features. Our predictions for abundance patterns provide initial insights, with variations stemming from the characteristics of the participating galaxies and the integration time. According to our models, the most pronounced effects of merger-driven accretion are seen in outer regions, giving rise to metal-rich stellar generation through gas that has been subject to gravitational manipulations. Ultimately, our research highlights the profound impact of major mergers on galaxy evolution, driving structural changes and altering stellar composition in a way that resonates across the galaxy's breadth. Nonetheless, our analysis also underscores the distinct influence of merger phases and remnants on galaxy development. By constraining the utz parameter space using existing experimental data from neutrino physics, we analyze the impact on recently observed phenomena, such as anomalous water-scattering and certain beta decay processes. Our calculations suggest that the utz theory can potentially explain the neutrino mass hierarchy, as predicted by the "just-so" model, without requiring an excessively large utz scale. Furthermore, we find that this theory could also contribute significantly to neutrino flavor-changing processes in certain scenarios. Additionally, we explore the possibility of utz contributing to dark matter in the early universe, and our results indicate that this could be compatible with the existence of neutrino modulus as dark matter in the present day. Specifically, we used a neural program model to evaluate the benefits of incorporating analyzer-supplied information about program validity and potential errors. Our results showed that this approach significantly enhanced program accuracy, both with and without external libraries, and included an analysis of various supervision levels and program types. Our data indicates that neural programs can produce substantially fewer errors when aided by analyzer-supplied information about program validity and potential errors, and that this advantage extends to programs that utilize external libraries. Furthermore, our results revealed that neural programs benefit from supervision that highlights potential hazards, and can produce more accurate programs when subjected to supervision at specific program nodes. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that neural programs can produce accurate programs when aided by even a basic level of supervision from a static program analyzer, and suggest that this may be a viable strategy for addressing one of the key challenges associated with neural programs - ensuring their safety and viability. The proposed method effectively handles growing datasets and enhances anomaly detection accuracy. Deep learning techniques are effective at recognizing this type of information but require extensive training data and a well-structured label system. This study introduces MetaFEND, a novel model that uses a unique, three-stage labeling approach to provide fine-grained feedback for machine learning models. Unlike traditional labeling methods that rely on expert assessments, MetaFEND's approach involves three types of non-expert labelers with distinct roles in stage one (claim evaluation) and stage two (counter-evidence assessment), and stage three (truth judgment). Our evaluation shows that providing fine-grained feedback through these stages leads to significant improvements in the performance of machine learning models, particularly in detecting false information. Our results demonstrate that even with relatively simple machine learning models, MetaFEND's approach yields impressive outcomes, showcasing the potential for this method to become a standard for labeling techniques. The study's findings also highlight potential limitations of the approach, such as the challenge of motivating non-expert labelers to provide high-quality feedback. To address this issue, we developed an incentive mechanism that encourages labelers to provide accurate feedback by following a simple scoring system. This paper compares the average age of information (AoI) in discrete and continuous time systems that maintain update histories at their inputs and output nodes. We model the AoI evolution in discrete time as a multi-dimensional random walk with uniform updates, leading to an analytical expression for the stationary AoI distribution. In contrast, the AoI process for continuous time systems can be defined as a pair of independent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, which enables us to derive the stationary AoI distribution in a closed form. Interestingly, the discrete time AoI distribution outpaces the continuous time AoI distribution, and this accelerated growth indicates that systems experience increased information aging as time progresses. To mitigate this effect, we can employ a linear aging reduction technique, which translates to a linear aging control approach in continuous time systems, resulting in a reduced stationary AoI distribution out of pace with time. Finally, we explore various system designs, including those involving noise at the input and output, and provide corresponding Age of Information (AoI) analyses. These scenarios, along with the proposed aging reduction technique, are then applied to typical communication protocols, such as TCP and HTTP. In response to these scenarios, we also present new communication protocols that minimize AoI and demonstrate the benefits of our results through numerical simulations. In doing so, we establish the foundation for future research in the field of AoI. In particular, we outline the challenges and opportunities associated with studying the AoI distribution in more complex systems and underscore the significance of innovative modeling techniques in this context. In addition, we highlight the scope for interdisciplinary research fueled by the AoI paradigm and inspired by our work. In the process, we clarify the relationship between AoI and other performance metrics commonly used in communication systems, such as delay, throughput, and reliability, and outline potential research directions that aim to reconcile these aspects. Ultimately, our examination of discrete and continuous time systems, coupled with our consideration of system designs and communication protocols, serves as a springboard for a broader exploration of theoretical and practical aspects of AoI in complex networks. As such, this study positions itself as a foundational contribution with far-reaching implications for the study and development of communication systems under the AoI performance criterion. In this context, we propose a number of research directions that aim to address fundamental questions in this field, and in doing so, we introduce novel models, techniques, and challenges that have the potential to shape the future of communication system design. We offer an in-depth examination of Drinfeld's twist theory, both set-theoretically and in the context of quantum deformations, and investigate how admissible Drinfeld twists are classified under these conditions. Our research reveals that both in set-theoretic and quantum contexts, admissible Drinfeld twists exhibit similar behavior, being in a bijective correspondence to the admissible elements of the first cohomology group of the Drinfeld algebra. To construct admissible Drinfeld twists, specific constraints must be satisfied. These constraints are given by a combination of the classical and quantum bijectivity conditions, as well as the classifying group's action. By exploring the classification of admissible Drinfeld twists, we are also able to derive the requirements for both set-theoretic and quantum deformations to be 'faithful'. Finally, our work establishes the connection between the set-theoretic and quantum deformations, and provides the classification of admissible Drinfeld twists at the quantum level when the base field has characteristic zero. This research is a continuation of the authors' previous work on this topic, and is intended to be a self-contained exposition. It is hoped that this new perspective will be able to facilitate the comparison of different construction methods for admissible Drinfeld twists. Additionally, this study is expected to be relevant to the broader context of non-deformed quantum group cohomology, and has already been shown to be relevant to the discussion of admissible Drinfeld twists through their relationship with the first cohomology group of the Drinfeld algebra. As such, this research is expected to be of particular interest to those with a focus on the interactions between algebra and quantum information theories. As part of this investigation, a comprehensive overview is also provided of the key developments in Drinfeld's twist theory, and its related extensions, with particular attention to the underlying constraints, construction methods, and related cohomology groups. This review is intended to be both concise and comprehensive, and is presented as a standalone discussion to facilitate ease of reference. We investigated the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction in a silicon crystal lattice with dopants, considering various substitution patterns for the nearest and next nearest neighbor spins. A comprehensive study was conducted for up to fifth nearest neighbor spins. Our analysis reveals a significant impact of dopant placement on the Heisenberg interaction, influenced by the presence of s-type spin orbit coupled orbitals at the dopant sites. A detailed analysis of the spin exchange interaction parameters revealed that the Heisenberg model can be applied to a silicon spin valve, allowing for control of the magnetic interaction between neighboring spins via a nearby tunnel barrier. Furthermore, we determined the influence of light on the system through s-type spin orbit coupled orbitals at the dopant sites. A thorough comparison was made between substitution patterns, including a proposed method using only next nearest neighbor spins, which could provide a simpler, yet effective, description of the Heisenberg model. A discussion on possible implementations and the influence of other physical effects on the Heisenberg interaction in silicon spin systems was also presented. We introduce a novel method called High-dimensional Structure Recovery (HSR) that enables a probabilistic model to learn the underlying structure of a new system based on time series data and limited categorical feedback. We have developed a specific probabilistic inference framework using a probabilistic neural network that can be trained to mimic the time series generation process. Our goal is to establish the theoretical foundation for Structure Recovery by demonstrating that our model allows for the extraction of underlying structure features from time series data. We have conducted experiments under varying conditions to validate the effectiveness of our HSR approach. Results show that HSR can effectively recover underlying structure and is robust to different data configurations. Furthermore, we have found that HSR can leverage categorical feedback to enhance structure recovery accuracy. We have also analyzed the interplay between structure recovery and probabilistic inference within our framework. Finally, we have explored applications of our HSR approach, including system visualization, policy development, and the impact of categorical feedback on system dynamics. We have introduced a public dataset and methods for evaluating our HSR approach. These contributions will facilitate future research in this area. We have made our code and dataset publicly available.

This work builds on the recent discovery of the graded Leibuzzitz rule by the authors and the finding of the graded Hilbert polynomial by the researchers mentioned in [11]. We demonstrate that the graded Hilbert polynomial identifies a key set of polynomials called 'E-polynomials' which closely resemble the stable homotopy invariants known as the Lannes functor values. These values are obtained from the graded ring of invariants through the action of a finite group on a polynomial ring, a key tool being the development of an explicit algorithm to compute the graded Hilbert polynomial. We further establish a connection between E-polynomials and the stable homotopy theory by interpreting certain partition indices as the coefficients of a product representation of E-polynomials, and show in a specific case that this index pattern shares a symmetric relationship with the Mumford invariants. We conclude by suggesting that the graded Hilbert polynomial, when indexed by partition sets, may serve as a general framework for interpreting various stable homotopy invariants. This framework would extend beyond the E-polynomials to cover the mu-invariants of self-map functions of complex projective manifolds, and possibly the stable homotopy invariants of Calder da Pinto and Ray. We also explore potential applications to the stable homotopy tables of rational cohomology diagrams. Moreover, we illustrate the computational benefits of this approach via a sample calculation of the graded Hilbert polynomial for the dihedral group D4, and analyse the resulting E-polynomial coefficients in the context of the extended power construction. As astrobiology searches expand to planetary systems beyond our solar system, using the tens of thousands of exoplanets discovered so far, the need for efficient and risk-free asteroid trajectories emerges. I present a novel, hybrid optimization technique that combines evolutionary computation with global optimization methods to create safe and energy-efficient asteroid trajectories for massive spectroscopic surveys. I demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by comparing it to traditional methods using a hypothetical Astrobiology Search Telescope capable of observing 5,000 targets in one hour. Results show that my hybrid technique finds trajectories 50-70% more efficient and 20-30% safer than standard methods, with optimization times similar to traditional methods. To showcase the algorithm's capabilities, I apply it to real-world targets and observe similar improvements in trajectory quality. Furthermore, I demonstrate that my hybrid technique can handle large datasets with 10,000 to 150,000 targets by achieving a 20-50% increase in efficiency and a 10-20% reduction in error for unsolved cases. The algorithm's success stems from its ability to create diverse initial conditions that, through global optimization, yield both optimal solutions and safer trajectories. This technique has the potential to significantly contribute to the discovery of biosignatures in exoplanet spectra.

We discuss the technical aspects of these methods and provide a computational algorithm for solving the associated optimization problems. We also examine the statistical properties of GHL and GFL under mild assumptions, demonstrating that both methods yield consistent estimates and facilitate variable selection. Additionally, we differentiate our proposals from other methods, such as Group Lasso, which assumes independence between groups, and discuss various applications, including binary classification, where our methods can be applied using logistic regression. We evaluate the performance of our methods through simulated data and a real-world dataset, presenting the results in our research findings. This study examines how classical partial differential equation (PDE) models are extended to nonlocal versions, with the focus on their kinetic relationships. As the nonlocal interaction kernel becomes localized, these nonlocal models converge to their classical PDE counterparts. To establish this convergence, we employ regularity gains induced by the nonlocal equation and a compactness argument, yielding bounded solutions when the kernel is localized. This approach facilitates the study of nonlocal diffusion-type equations within the recently developed general framework. Additionally, we investigate the well-posedness of nonlocal parabolic equations and discuss the role of localization in determining the global boundedness of solutions. As the nonlocal diffusion model is known to exhibit similar behavior to the classical Cahn-Hilliard equation in terms of global boundedness, it is conceivable that both the nonlocal Cahn-Hilliard equation and its classical counterpart share the same minimizer when considering the energy functional. However, we demonstrate that this common minimizer is not uniquely chosen in energy, but rather depends on the specific kernel used in the nonlocal version. This dependence on kernel is used to further illustrate the distinct properties of nonlocal equations through specific examples, demonstrating how these examples can produce different classical limits, revealing the inherent sensitivity of the nonlocal equation to its kernel parameter. Consequently, we conclude that any general classical limit for these nonlocal equations cannot be unique. As a result, we propose distinguishing limits for particular nonlocal equations as $\sigma \to \delta$, advocating for classifications based on whether these limits encompass or exclude classical solutions. As an illustration, we show that particular nonlocal equations encompass classical solutions for both localized and nonlocalized interaction kernels. Moreover, we demonstrate that certain nonlocal equations exhibit distinct classical limits depending on the classification of the kernel, specifically distinguishing between Monge-Ampere type and Mckean-Vlasov type equations. As such, we propose a new framework for classifying these nonlocal equations based on their classical limit properties. As an additional outcome, we derive an implicit formula for the first order nonlocal parabolic equation within the generalized gradient flow framework, thereby establishing an explicit relationship between the nonlocal velocity field and the difference of states. Additionally, we establish global boundedness of solutions for the nonlocal parabolic equation under localized kernels, while demonstrating that when the kernel is nonlocalized, solutions may become unbounded in finite time, providing an alternative proof of the recent result by Simonett and Yang. Recent advancements in computer vision have enabled efficient and accurate panoramic image capture using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN). Nonetheless, real-world applications also necessitate accurate and constant lighting conditions to maintain visual authenticity. Our proposed system integrates Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) with CNN-based panoramic image capture, allowing for automatic lighting normalization. By leveraging the data generated by IMUs, our system can determine the position, orientation, and capture duration for each image, thereby facilitating the creation of a realistic day-night panorama. Moreover, our system incorporates a lighting normalization module, which utilizes the captured images and IMU data to create a lighting map. This map can then be applied to the original day-night images, yielding a realistic day-night panorama. Experimental results demonstrate our system's capability to produce high-quality day-night panormas, either with moderate (e.g. cafe) or extreme (e.g. day-night) lighting changes. We offer an open source Python 3.6 framework for generating artificial images to classify, using super pixel delimiting masks. Our framework is versatile, allowing for various data augmentation techniques to be applied to multiple object detection algorithms. It utilizes a Convolutional Neural Network to predict masks within an image, which are then utilized to create artificial images when combined with actual image data. This framework has demonstrated a three percent enhancement in accuracy when testing with artificial images produced via mask application against regular data augmentation methods. Furthermore, it has achieved a twenty percent enhancement in accuracy when testing with limited artificial images, compared to conventional data augmentation techniques. This framework comprises 3000 artificial images, created via mask application, that are usable for the Bird Species Classification task. It has specifically been designed to augment the work of the Bird Classification Competition, yet it may also be adapted for usage in other object classification contexts. The source code and artificial images are available for use at https://github.com/protopopescu/Bird_Species_Augmentation. The framework comprises two primary modules:
-   **mask_utils**: This module is responsible for the application and manipulation of masks. It utilizes the scikit-learn library to fit a Convolutional Neural Network for predicting masks within images, which are in RGB format. It also utilizes the OpenCV library to apply and adjust the masks.
-   **data_augmentation**: This module is responsible for the generation of artificial images via mask application. It utilizes the OpenCV library to split super pixels, apply artificial images, and combine actual and artificial image data.

This framework has been designed with consideration for its adaptability, making it suitable for usage with various object detection algorithms, such as YOLO, Faster R-CNN, and Deeper. It has also been devised with a modular structure in mind, allowing for the integration of additional data augmentation techniques. Ultimately, this framework has demonstrated its effectiveness in enhancing the accuracy of Convolutional Neural Networks via image classification tests conducted with both artificial and limited artificial images. The anisotropic capacity is shown to be compatible with anisotropic Hardy-Littlewood maximal operators and anisotropic fractional maximal operators. Additionally, the anisotropic capacity is linked to established volumetric inequalities, including the anisotropic Poincar\'{e} inequality and the anisotropic Sobolev inequality. The anisotropic capacity is also proven to be equivalent to the anisotropic Reifenberg type capacity and the anisotropic Riesz capacity, providing a bridge between different anisotropic geometric analysis inequalities and the anisotropic capacity. The anisotropic capacity is analyzed in relation to anisotropic isoperimetric inequalities, an anisotropic log-Harnack inequality, an anisotropic Colding-Nirenberg inequality, and an anisotropic quantitative soliton inequality. The anisotropic capacity is demonstrated to be a fundamental concept unifying various anisotropic geometric analysis inequalities and could be a significant tool for further research in this field.

Identifying and correcting sudden, anonymous events, known as glitches, in a space-borne acceleration sensor experiment is a crucial challenge. These spikes, resulting from the sensor's inherent flaws or external interference, contaminating accurate acceleration data and jeopardizing the overall measurement reliability. Determining the distribution and statistical properties of these glitches in relation to radiation exposure in orbit is, therefore, essential for a comprehensive understanding of in-orbit radiation effects. For a marked tree defined by randomly selecting a root and using it to build a tree under the rule of consistent ordering, we analyze the structure of the tree and the associated frog process. Depending on the degree of the tree, which is denoted by $\delta$, we examine how the tree transitions from a transient state to a recurrent state. It is found that when the degree $\delta$ is greater than 1, the tree is transient, providing a more general condition than a previous requirement for the degree to be greater than 2. Furthermore, we prove that as the number of leaves increases, the structure of the tree evolves from a transient state to a recurrent state. We then discuss how this transition is related to the scaling limit of a critical unbiased random walk on the tree, which is known to converge to a Brownian motion. Additionally, we present arguments suggesting that the tree, which is constructed by applying a ordering rule to a binary sequence, shares the same properties as a free group grassmanian graph, which is known to have a similar structure. We also derive an upper bound for the highest transience threshold of the tree, which is $\delta \geq 3$, and discuss how this threshold is greater than the lowest conductivity threshold of the tree, which is $\delta \geq 2$. Furthermore, we establish that the ratio of these two thresholds tends to 4 as the degree of the tree increases infinitely, which provides a quadruple confirmation of the superuniversal property of the free group. Barabasi-Albert models, duals of ordered trees, and planar maps with a degree sequence are also discussed as additional examples. Through analyzing dynamic or stochastic processes on these trees, we are able to draw general conclusions about the behavior of these processes when the degree of the tree increases infinitely. Finally, we discuss possible directions for applying the techniques used in this paper to analyze the structure of trees in greater depth.

In recent years, knowledge distillation has proven to be a highly effective method for black-box compression. While traditional approaches successfully leverage a surrogate model's responses to guide a student model towards better performance, the concept of knowledge distillation is expanding to incorporate new strategies that target specific queries. One such innovative approach, decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, assumes that a knowledgeable model's ability to make informed decisions is valuable and can be learned from a black-box model's choices. Unlike the knowledge distillation methods discussed in the literature, DB3 does not rely on a surrogate model to provide labeled responses, instead it uses the black-box model's decisions in relation to the queries being optimized. One key challenge in DB3 is developing a suitable loss function to capture the knowledge contained in decision-making processes. To address this, we analyze the relationship between model decisions and classify them as relative or absolute knowledge. Based on this distinction, we propose two general frameworks, one for relative decision-based knowledge distillation and the other for absolute decision-based knowledge distillation. To bridge the gap between theoretical frameworks and practical applications, we examine decision-based knowledge distillation in the context of ranking tasks, specifically web ranking. By formulating the loss function in relation to the submodularity maximization problem, we demonstrate the feasibility of DB3 in this domain. Experimental results show that decision-based knowledge distillation can learn from a search engine's ranking decisions and develop a highly effective student model for web ranking. Moreover, we explore various decision-based knowledge distillation strategies and evaluate their efficacy in other ranking tasks. Our research on decision-based knowledge distillation offers a range of possibilities for compressing various black-box models through query-based compression, and we look forward to seeing the innovative applications and extensions of this concept in the future. Policy optimization via imitation from raw video data is highly desirable for unsupervised learning, yet currently, we lack a systematic approach for evaluating and improving sample efficiency in this context. The problem lies in the absence of a suitable baseline algorithm for comparison, given that most imitation learning methods are developed with the assumption of labeled data in mind. To address this issue, we introduce the TRAIL framework, which treats sample efficiency as a problem of transfer learning between distributions. By doing so, we establish a metric to evaluate the efficiency of an algorithm in one distribution setting, without requiring labeled data in the target distribution. Utilizing TRAIL, we conduct a comprehensive study of sample efficiency in imitation learning, involving various algorithms and scenarios, and provide a unified framework for understanding the results. Our experiments demonstrate that TRAIL provides a coherent evaluation of sample efficiency in imitation learning, enabling us to identify the strengths and limitations of existing algorithms. Moreover, we discover that some algorithms exhibit greater efficiency in certain scenarios, despite being developed with the assumption of labeled data in mind. To further investigate this phenomenon, we develop the TRAIL algorithm, which achieves notable improvements in sample efficiency, outperforming existing methods by factor of up to five in certain scenarios. The success of TRAIL is attributed to an enhanced exploration strategy, featuring a middle-ground explorer that balances the exploitation of learned policies with the exploration of new actions. We showcase the TRAIL algorithm's superiority in scenarios involving a real-world application, namely human-robot collaboration, without requiring labeled data in the target distribution. To facilitate future research, we publicly release the code, data, and evaluation metrics for the TRAIL framework. Through the TRAIL framework, we hope to stimulate a systematic discussion on sample efficiency in imitation learning, while providing a foundation for advancing research in this context. By leveraging both online interactions with rewards-based feedback and off-line data, the system uses two efficient components to achieve optimal policy updates. 

Unlike traditional methods that require extensive expert input, our proposed solution addresses the lack of available demonstrations by dividing the process into two parts: a reliable expert advisor and a transitional learner. 

Experimental results on complex games demonstrate that our co-imitation learning framework outperforms not only conventional imitation learning but also expert-critic methods, where the only input required is the game outcome. 

Notably, our proposal enhances the efficiency of policy updates with optimal quadratic regression and both online and off-line data, as evidenced by the significant reduction in required demonstrations.

We suggest that the challenge of large action spaces in sequence-to-sequence reinforcement learning can be addressed by reducing actions to a more manageable set, potentially leading to improved performance. To achieve this, we propose a novel paradigm where actions are learned as latent variables rather than fixed output tokens. We apply this approach to a prominent machine translation task and demonstrate that our method not only effectively mitigates the action space issue but also yields substantially better performance. The key components of our model include an action encoder that leverages an additional encoder module, a latent action generator, and a transition model. We utilize a straightforward alternative to high-dimensional policy evaluation methods to devise a efficient reward estimator. Our model's performance is consistently superior to baseline methods across multiple settings. Moreover, we highlight that our action-generation approach superior to prior methods handling large action spaces. We further show that our method's performance is highly robust to different value function architectures, surpassing baseline methods under minimal extraction scenarios. Our method's best performance is achieved when transition models are incorporated, and this is further highlighted by our results on a large-scale low-latency machine translation task. We publicly release our dataset, along with the code and models, to facilitate further research in this area. Our method's code can be found at https://github.com/ghrua/latent-action-rl. Accurate end-effector pose estimation is crucial in robot operations and a key factor in achieving this is through robust on-board sensing systems that can stabilize the end-effector during calibration. To enhance the reliability of this process, our proposed approach utilizes a depth camera to capture the environment from the end-effector's perspective, thereby increasing the stability of the end-effector during calibration. The introduced system leverages a single CMOS depth camera to obtain multiple, simultaneously captured images, which are then analyzed using an object recognition algorithm to estimate the end-effector's pose. The system's performance was optimized by conducting experiments using a robotic arm equipped with a depth camera, and the results showed that our approach can estimate the end-effector's pose with high accuracy, even when the end-effector is subjected to sudden movements, by processing previously stored data from stable pose captures. To further demonstrate the system's calibration capabilities, we designed an automated testing setup, which validated the system's performance through multiple tests, resulting in an average pose estimation error of less than 5 degrees. The developed system has potential applications in various industries, such as the calibration of surgical tools for enhanced surgical outcomes, and is comprised of a modular design, allowing for customizable development, along with publicly available code, which can be adapted for different calibration tasks. The system's code is openly accessible on GitHub, and we have released a demonstration video of the system in action on YouTube. The system's design can be found in the attached document, which includes the layout of the modular structure, the calibration process, and the object recognition algorithm.
